papers.title: Andreev Beta Conversion and Bulk Viscosity in Superfluid Neutron-Star Matter
papers.summary: Bulk viscosity in neutron-star matter is attributed to the phase lag between a density oscillation and weak beta equilibration. We point out a distinct coherent channel when the baryonic component that stores the condensate is superfluid: an effective beta-conversion event between a neutron condensate and normal protons can proceed as an Andreev process, converting a particle-like excitation into a hole-like excitation while adding or removing a Cooper pair from the condensate. The resulting Andreev contribution to beta equilibration is fourth order in the effective conversion vertex, is enhanced by anomalous neutron Green's functions, and is not captured by standard Urca process. We identify the density, temperature, and oscillation-frequency regimes where this channel can dominate viscous damping of neutron-star oscillations and mergers.

We find that [WR] central stars are closer to the Galactic plane than hydrogen-rich central stars and than other hydrogen-poor central stars. The latter have a similar distribution to hydrogen-rich central stars, which is significantly different from the one of [WR] central stars. This result disagrees with the proposed evolutionary sequence for hydrogen-poor central stars.

papers.title: Galaxy Luminosity Function of the Coma Cluster from Deep $u'-g'-r'$ Wendelstein Imaging Data
papers.summary: We derive the $g'$ band galaxy luminosity function (GLF) of quenched resolved galaxies in the Coma cluster from a deep-imaging survey with $\approx1.5\,\mathrm{deg^2}$ around the cluster center. The dataset comprises deep $u'$-, $g'$-, and $r'$-band data obtained with the Wendelstein Wide Field Imager on the $2.1\,\mathrm{m}$ Fraunhofer Wendelstein Telescope reaching median $3\sigma$ surface brightness limits in 10" $\times$ 10" boxes of $\mathrm{ (30.0\,u',\,\,29.6\,g',\,\,28.7\,r')\,mag\,arcsec^{-2}}$. We measure structural parameters across a large dynamic range in galaxy brightness ($-24.5\,g'\,\mathrm{mag} \lessapprox M\lessapprox-11.3\,g'\,\mathrm{mag}$), from the brightest cluster galaxy to low-luminosity dwarfs, including compact dwarf galaxies and ultra-diffuse galaxies. We automatically identify more than 6000 cluster member candidates based on their membership on the quiescent sequence in the $u'-g'$ versus $g'-r'$ color--color diagram. The structural parameters of bright galaxies are obtained via isophotal modeling, and fully automated parametric image fitting for faint ones. Injection-recovery tests and two identically analyzed reference fields provide statistical corrections for completeness and contamination, yielding a representative GLF that reliably probes the faint end and may serve as a benchmark for future studies. We report a best-fit single Schechter $g'$ band GLF with $M^*=-21.60^{+0.25}_{-0.27}\,g'\,\mathrm{mag}$, $\log_{10}(\phi^*\,[\mathrm{deg}^{-2}\,\mathrm{mag}^{-1}])=1.378^{+0.076}_{-0.081}$, and a comparatively steep faint-end slope $\alpha=-1.445^{+0.016}_{-0.017}$. A directly matched comparison with the Coma counterpart in SLOW, a constrained cosmological simulation using CDM, shows broad agreement between the GLFs down to the simulation limit of $M = -15.5\,g'\,\mathrm{mag}$, despite a deficit of bright galaxies.

papers.title: Hydrodynamic instabilities in long-term three-dimensional simulations of neutrino-driven supernovae of 13 red supergiant progenitors
papers.summary: We present long-term three-dimensional (3D) simulations of Type-IIP supernovae (SNe) for 13 non-rotating, single-star, red-supergiant (RSG) progenitors with zero-age-main-sequence masses between 12.5 M$_{\odot}$ and 27.3 M$_{\odot}$. The explosions were modelled with a parametric treatment of neutrino heating to obtain defined energies, ${}^{56}$Ni yields, and neutron-star properties in agreement with previous results. Our 3D SN models were evolved from core bounce until 10 days to study how the large-scale mixing of chemical elements depends on the progenitor structure. Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities (RTIs), which grow at the (C+O)/He and He/H interfaces and interact with the reverse shock forming after the SN shock has passed the He/H interface, play a crucial role in the outward mixing of ${}^{56}$Ni into the hydrogen envelope. We find most extreme ${}^{56}$Ni mixing and the highest maximum ${}^{56}$Ni velocities in lower-mass (LM) explosions despite lower explosion energies, and the weakest ${}^{56}$Ni mixing in the 3D explosions of the most massive RSGs. The efficiency of radial ${}^{56}$Ni mixing anti-correlates linearly with the helium-core mass and correlates positively with the magnitude of a local maximum of $\rho r^3$ in the helium shell. This maximum causes shock deceleration and therefore facilitates high growth factors of RTI at the (C+O)/He interface in the LM explosions. Therefore fast-moving ${}^{56}$Ni created by the asymmetric neutrino-heating mechanism is carried into the ubiquitous RT-unstable region near the He/H interface and ultimately far into the envelopes of the exploding RSGs. Our correlations may aid improving mixing prescriptions in 1D SN models and deducing progenitor structures from observed SN properties..

papers.title: Clustering effects on the Dark Siren determination of $H_0$: A simulation study
papers.summary: We investigate the cosmological power of gravitational wave (GWs) events without electromagnetic counterparts using high-resolution, cosmological simulations that include realistic clustering. We assume a near-future detector network (LVK + LIGO India in O5), with sky localisation and distance uncertainty capabilities for binary black holes, of the order of $60$ deg. squared and $10\%$ respectively, and with a range of about $1600$ Mpc/h. We find that clustering leads to increased convergence of the $H_0$ posteriors, with clear recovery of the input value as early as $N_{\rm gw}=40$ events (a very conservative estimate for O5, which expects thousands of BBHs/year). In contrast, even with $N_{\rm gw}=100$ events in uniform catalogues, the posterior remains largely unconstrained. Additionally, we quantify the role of catalogue completeness and show that levels as low as $f=25\%$ can be competitive with fully complete catalogues, confirming the impact of clustering. Completeness levels of $f=50\%$ perform statistically similar to complete catalogues with as few as $N_{\rm gw}=40$ events. We conclude that improving GWs detection capabilities yields better results than more complete galaxy catalogues.Finally, we find that 1) physical weights do not provide significant additional constraining power on top of clustering, 2) luminosity distance errors contribute more for small cone openings, 3) the $H_0$ prior range does not introduce any biases in the $H_0$ posterior, 4) closer events ($\lesssim 100$ Mpc/h) yield about two times better precision than more distant events ($\lesssim 1600$ Mpc/h), and 5) our method is robust to different modelling choices.

papers.title: A unified harmonic framework for dark siren cosmology
papers.summary: The galaxy catalog dark siren method aims to infer cosmological parameters from gravitational waves (GWs) without an electromagnetic counterpart by statistically marginalizing over possible host galaxies. The cross-correlation of GW sources and galaxies is a promising avenue for cosmological inference without requiring observed host galaxies, by leveraging 2-point statistics. We provide a detailed guide to the cross-correlation method, clarifying its relationship to standard dark siren techniques as well as the assumptions necessary to be able to use this formalism on GW data. We show that a 2x2 point cross-correlation analysis extends the angular part of the galaxy catalog method transformed to harmonic space, in which the unknown galaxy field is marginalized over rather than treated as fixed and uniform. Combined with the spectral sirens method, which encodes information from the GW rate evolution, mass distribution, and selection effects, one can perform an inference that leverages the joint constraining power of all dark siren methods. We also present a strategy to rigorously fold GW measurement errors into the likelihood. Using this method, we show that with a 2 Einstein Telescope + 1 Cosmic Explorer setup, the GW--galaxy cross-correlation part alone can jointly measure $H_0$ and $\Omega_{m, 0}$ to $1\%$ and $5\%$ precision with just 2 years of data, demonstrating its potential as a precise and scalable inference technique in the next generation of GW and galaxy surveys. This is in contrast with canonical hierarchical Bayesian population inference techniques, which are known to scale poorly with the precision and catalog size expected of next-generation GW experiments. Because the cross-correlation method implicitly requires large-number statistics, a GW--galaxy cross-correlation measurement is not possible with current GW catalogs.

papers.title: Can current models predict the local black hole merger rate?
papers.summary: After four observational runs, the Ligo-Virgo-Kagra collaboration estimated a local binary black hole (BBH) merger rate density of $R_{0,\textrm{LVK}}\simeq 14-26\,\textrm{Gpc}^{-3}\,\textrm{yr}^{-1}$ within the 90% credible interval. Some previous studies already pointed out that, when a realistic evolution of the metallicity-dependent cosmic star formation rate density (SFRD) is adopted, theoretical models predict a local BBH merger rate density that exceeds the observed value by at least a factor of $\sim 10$. In this paper, we confirm and strengthen this claim by constructing an empirical model for the SFRD and metallicity evolution that includes a correction accounting for iron abundance. The adopted metallicity relation is flexible, enabling us to bracket the wide range of observational uncertainties. We show that, even under the most conservative assumptions regarding both the SFRD and the metallicity relation, the local BBH merger rate density is overestimated by a factor $> 10$. Attempts to reconcile the predicted and observed merger rates by modifying only the metallicity-dependent SFRD would require unrealistically high metallicities ($Z>Z_\odot$) even in low-mass galaxies at high redshift. This finding indicates that revisions to the treatment of stellar and binary evolution are necessary to achieve consistency between theoretical predictions and observations. We suggest that even a modest steepening of the delay-time distribution could help alleviate this tension.

papers.title: Constraints with CMB lensing on dark matter decays to massive decay products
papers.summary: Motivated by the recent measurements by the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) which suggest a late-time matter density approximately 5\% lower than that inferred from Planck we investigate models in which dark matter decays to two less massive, and thus warm, states. The decaying dark matter (DDM) models are parameterized by the fraction $f$ of dark matter that decays, the decay rate $\Gamma$, and the fraction $\varepsilon$ of the mass retained by the decay products. To efficiently explore the warm decay product regime, we employ \texttt{CLASSIER-DDM}, a modified version of the public Boltzmann solver \texttt{CLASS} that solves the perturbation equations with DDM via an integral-equation method. We consider DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations and Planck 2018 CMB data including lensing, and find that DDM models are not favored over the $\Lambda$CDM model. This result arises because CMB lensing tightly constrains the velocity kicks imparted to decay products. For example, for $f\simeq0.5$, we find $1\sigma$ constraints to the decay-product kick velocities an order of $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-3}$ times the speed of light for decay redshifts from shortly after recombination until today. Nonetheless, the allowed parameter space includes models with sufficient power suppression at small-scales to potentially address dwarf galaxy anomalies. Our results also suggest that explanations for DESI that involve dark-matter decays to one massive and one massless particle will be constrained by CMB lensing.

papers.title: Cosmological constraints from the DESI DR1 Bispectrum Full-Shape and DR2 BAO
papers.summary: We present cosmological constraints from DESI DR1 full-shape measurements, including the LRG bispectrum, combined with DESI DR2 BAO data. The analysis accounts for cross-covariance using mocks, while ShapeFit compression mitigates prior volume effects in beyond-$\Lambda$CDM analyses. In $\Lambda$CDM, the DESI1.5 (P+B) analysis yields $\sigma_8=0.868\pm0.026$ and $S_8=0.880\pm0.028$, compared with $\sigma_8=0.822\pm0.034$ and $S_8=0.827\pm0.036$ in the previous power-spectrum-only analysis. The marginalized uncertainties are reduced by 24% and 22%, respectively. For $w_0w_a$CDM, DESI-only analyses with the bispectrum shift dark energy parameters toward $\Lambda$CDM, consistent with a cosmological constant within $1\sigma$ in the $w_0$--$w_a$ plane. Adding CMB creates a preference for evolving dark energy: DESI+CMB (P+B) shows a $2.8\sigma$ deviation from $\Lambda$CDM. Including DES-Dovekie supernovae alone reduces this to $1.6\sigma$, while the full combination gives $3.1\sigma$. The bispectrum weakens evidence for time-varying dark energy relative to power-spectrum-only analyses. It also enhances sensitivity to massive neutrinos: in DESI-only data, the power-spectrum-only posterior for $\sum m_\nu$ is consistent with zero, whereas adding the bispectrum yields $0.26\pm0.18$ eV and a 95% upper limit of $0.59$ eV, shifting the peak into the positive region. For modified gravity, the bispectrum constrains $\mu_0 = 0.12\pm0.51$ from DESI-only data, consistent with general relativity.

papers.title: Transition from Diffusion to Drift-Dominated Cosmic Ray Transport and the Origin of the Knee
papers.summary: In a magnetic field with a complex topology, as can be the Galactic magnetic field, cosmic ray transport cannot simply be described by diffusion parallel and perpendicular to magnetic field lines, because the gradients and curvature of the large-scale magnetic field induce drift motions. These effects become especially important at high energies. Here we revisit the possibility that the competition between diffusion and drifts may lead to a knee in the cosmic ray spectrum. We carry out test-particle simulations of cosmic ray transport in a mock Galactic magnetic field made of a regular large scale component, with a non-trivial topology and a homogeneous and isotropic turbulent magnetic field, with a spectrum that is assumed to be Kolmogorov-like in the basic setup. These simulations are used to infer the escape time and the grammage accumulated by cosmic rays with energy in the TeV--10 PeV energy range. In the case of a large scale magnetic field with a purely azimuthal structure, the drift due to the curvature of magnetic field lines produces a knee in the PeV range, but the model fails to reproduce the grammage, due to the exceedingly low value of the perpendicular diffusion coefficient. If the large scale magnetic field acquires a component perpendicular to the Galactic disc, the parallel diffusion coefficient becomes quickly dominant in terms of particle escape, and drifts are unable to compete. A knee structure does not appear in such a scenario. However, if the parallel diffusion coefficient becomes energy independent at $E\gtrsim 1$ TeV, a knee may arise around PeV energies due to drift dominance. We discuss two cases in which this situation may occur.

papers.title: FRANZ: Framework for analytical one-zone blastwave dynamics
papers.summary: (abridged) We develop a flexible analytical framework for modeling blastwave evolution in arbitrary environments and use it to investigate how large-scale galactic structure affects the dynamics and morphology of evolved SNRs and SBs. We introduce FRANZ (FRamework for ANalytical one-Zone blastwave dynamics), a modular thin-shell model that follows the local evolution of a shock-surface segment in environments characterized by arbitrary density, velocity and gravitational fields. After validating the model against well-established analytical results, we apply it to study the effects of vertical stratification, galactic shear and dense galactic substructure on blastwave evolution. FRANZ reproduces the classical evolution of blastwaves in uniform media while extending to complex environments. We derive criteria for disk break out in stratified media, characterize the timescales on which differential rotation deforms blastwaves and identify a new mechanism, by which it can suppress the momentum coupling in continuously-driven blastwaves. Interactions with dense filaments modify both shock-surface morphology and dynamics and confound the interpretation of the expansion history of observed remnants, which depends on the density distribution prior to the onset of explosions, which is fundamentally inaccessible from the observed state. In highly structured media with a high volume-filling factor of diffuse gas, ages inferred from the observed state may be systematically overestimated. FRANZ provides a computationally inexpensive and extensible framework for studying blastwaves in realistic galactic environments. It offers a useful complement to numerical simulations for interpreting observations of evolved SNRs and SBs and for developing improved models of stellar feedback in large-scale simulations.

papers.title: Gas Motions in Hydra-A: XRISM Constraints on ICM Kinematics Across Jet-Inflated Cavities
papers.summary: We report on two deep XRISM observations of the central and northern regions of Hydra-A's X-ray atmosphere, covering the bubbles inflated by jets from the central galaxy's active galactic nucleus. We use spatial-spectral mixing, combining Chandra's high spatial resolution with XRISM's high spectral resolution, to investigate atmospheric kinematics. The velocity dispersion in the northern region, $\sigma_v = 140^{+30}_{-20}$ km s$^{-1}$, is comparable to that in the central region ($\sigma_v = 162 \pm 10$ km s$^{-1}$). We show that motion of the large-scale cocoon shock front could be responsible for the large dispersion toward the north. The dispersion in the northeast quarter of the central pointing, $\sigma_v = 260 \pm 50$ km s$^{-1}$, is among the highest measured. This region contains an X-ray-bright feature previously identified as metal-rich, possibly gas uplifted in the wake of previous-generation cavities. Dispersions in all other quarter regions are low ($\sigma_v \leq 180$ km s$^{-1}$) and consistent with previous XRISM results from other objects. The kinetic energy at the center is comparable to the enthalpies of the cavities, while in the north it is roughly an order of magnitude smaller. The jet thus drives gas motion efficiently at smaller scales ($r < 95$ kpc) and inefficiently at larger scales ($95-317$ kpc toward the north along the jet). A bulk flow toward our line of sight of $-100 \pm 30$ km s$^{-1}$ in the southwest quarter of the central pointing, measured with respect to the central galaxy, is also observed, possibly due to sloshing. No significant bulk motion was detected in any other region.

papers.title: A Deep Look at the Ultra-Faint Milky Way Satellite Virgo III with Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2
papers.summary: We analyze the ultra-faint Milky Way satellite Virgo III using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2 (DP2). Virgo III was observed in the Rubin "Cosmic Treasure Chest" (M49) First Look field, which contains 924 visits in the u,g,r,i bands comprising ~10.5hrs of exposure time with LSSTCam. These data are considerably deeper than the majority of DP2, with a $5\sigma$ limiting magnitude that approaches the expected 10-year depth of LSST (~25.2-26.5mag, depending on band). We report the morphological and stellar population parameters of Virgo III measured with the maximum-likelihood-based package ugali. The depth of the Rubin imaging yields more than a factor of four increase in the number of candidate member stars ($N_* = 114^{+11}_{-11}$) relative to the Virgo III discovery results ($N_* = 25^{+5}_{-4}$), enabling significantly more precise morphological constraints. Our best-fit parameters broadly agree with previous measurements, further confirming that Virgo III has properties that are consistent with an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy ($M_V = -2.72^{+0.49}_{-0.70}$; $r_{1/2} = 53^{+10}_{-8}$) located at a heliocentric distance of $D_\odot = 151^{+8}_{-8}$. We also demonstrate that the depth and photometric quality of the DP2 data are sufficient to separate metal-poor and metal-rich stars in color-color space. We further present period estimates for the three known RR Lyrae member stars derived from the DP2 forced photometry; we use theoretical Period-Luminosity-Metallicity (PLZ) and Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity (PWZ) relations to obtain independent distance estimates. We find that our period and distance estimates are broadly consistent with previous measurements for these RR Lyrae. These results demonstrate the power of LSST data for the discovery and characterization of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and motivate future searches for new satellites across the southern sky.

papers.title: An ALMA study of hub-filament systems II.Quiescent filaments converging towards highly dynamic hubs
papers.summary: Hub-filament systems are networks of converging interstellar filaments, often with active star formation at their centres, that may play an important role in high-mass star formation. In the first paper of this series, we found that the mass fraction that ends up in a clump's most massive core is significantly higher in IR-dark hubs than in IR-bright clumps, suggesting that the most-massive cores form early on. Such early massive core formation requires large inflow rates and dynamically active IR-dark clumps. We now present N$_2$H$^+$(J=1-0) observations of six IR-dark hub-filament systems mapped with ALMA 12m, 7m, and total power at 3'' resolution, to trace the kinematics of the dense gas. The data show intricate emission structures and complex spectra. To characterise their kinematics, we have developed mwydyn, a fully-automated, multiple velocity component, hyperfine line-fitting code. Our results reveal that the emission invariably consists of quiescent individual filaments in the outskirts that converge towards the hub centres where a systematic increase in velocity dispersion and number of components is observed. We also find that the distribution of centroid velocities is remarkably similar between clumps, despite spanning more than one order of magnitude in mass. We propose that our results are best explained by the mixing of gravitationally-driven multi-directional inflows, resulting in highly complex and dynamic hub centres. We also discuss the implications of the observed differentiated filament and hub gas kinematics in the context of the 3D morphology of hub-filament systems.

papers.title: An "inside-out" approach to modeling supermassive black hole binary inspiral
papers.summary: The inspiral and merger of two supermassive black holes (SMBHs) releases immense energy in low-frequency gravitational waves (GWs). Recent pulsar timing array (PTA) observations of the stochastic nHz GW background (GWB) are consistent with a SMBH binary origin. GW data from PTAs and from the upcoming Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) can probe late-stage binary evolution where electromagnetic constraints are scarce. However, the complexity of the relevant astrophysics necessitates a well optimized approach. I argue that a key physical quantity to constrain with PTAs is the orbital semi-major axis at which binary inspiral transitions from the astrophysical to the GW-dominated regime ($a_{\rm GW}$). This quantity should be treated as a free parameter in analysis of the GWB. Using this premise, I present a simple analytic framework for modeling SMBH binary inspiral in an "inside-out" fashion. At orbital separations slightly larger than $a_{\rm GW}$, a power-law scaling for the astrophysical inspiral timescale is assumed, while the outermost phase (prior to the PTA regime) is simply modeled via a delay time. I show that the GWB spectral shape and amplitude are most sensitive to $a_{\rm GW}$ (normalized to $10^9 M_{\odot}$, equal-mass binaries and expressed in gravitational units), with weaker dependence on the inner power-law index and the outer delay time. The GWB is largely insensitive to the mass and mass-ratio scaling of $a_{\rm GW}$ and to the boundary between the inner and outer astrophysical inspiral regimes. I compare with models for gas- and stellar-driven binary inspiral and discuss implications for LISA and for GW source parameter inference.

papers.title: Bifrost spectral inversions: Fast non-LTE solar chromospheric diagnostics from 3D simulations
papers.summary: Modern solar observatories produce vast amounts of detailed spectral data. To infer atmospheric parameters from these data, in particular for the solar chromosphere, requires immense computational resources. This problem is becoming more acute as spatial resolution improves, and faster methods are much needed to make sense of the data. Archive-based inversions provide a cost-effective way to infer atmospheric parameters from solar spectra; they involve building databases of synthetic spectra and atmospheric models. We extended this idea to a k-nearest neighbour inversion with non-LTE chromospheric spectra from a 3D radiative-magnetohydrodynamic simulation. Our database consists of 150 million Ca II 8542 {\AA} line profiles from a magnetically quiet simulation. We validated our method on a different simulation and then applied the database inversion to high-cadence observations taken with the Swedish 1-m Solar Telescope. We find excellent agreement between the observed and fitted spectra for almost the entire field of view. We recovered the chromospheric temperature and line-of-sight velocity and calculated the uncertainty in their inversions. The gas temperature has small uncertainties over a broad range of optical depths, and we recover a physically consistent solution, even beyond the line sensitivity region. Compared with the traditional inversion method, our approach is four orders of magnitude faster. Limitations and future improvements of the method are discussed.

papers.title: HURACAN: A comparison of stellar and interstellar proper motions inside L1688
papers.summary: The assumption that molecular clouds are kinematically coupled to the young stellar populations forming within them is observationally still poorly constrained. With the transverse component $v_{\textrm{t}}$ of the interstellar medium (ISM) motion being largely unknown, the three-dimensional kinematic state of even the closest clouds remains incomplete. We provide the first direct measurement of the transverse motion of the ISM inside the Ophiuchus cloud L1688 and compare it with the kinematics of the surrounding young stellar populations. The measurement was obtained using intensity-based image registration applied to archival data, allowing us to generate a proper motion field of the studied regions and determine the cloud's bulk motion, $(\mu_{\alpha^*},\mu_\delta)^{\mathrm{ISM}}_{\mathrm{median}}=(-3.0, -24.1)$ mas yr$^{-1}$. This motion differs from the kinematics of the youngest population in Upper Scorpius by $3\pm1$ km s$^{-1}$, highlighting the possibility of a bias when using stars as a proxy for the ISM motion near star-forming regions. By comparing the cloud's motion with that of the youngest stellar population in the region and the B-star Oph S1 located within the cloud, we find that stellar feedback must have dynamically shaped the motion of the ISM over the last few million years. Furthermore, by studying a shell-like ISM structure appearing in L1688, we find evidence suggesting that this object is likely neither a typical Herbig-Haro object nor a supernova remnant, with its origin remaining a mystery. Our results demonstrate that archival and future high-resolution near-infrared observations can and will continue to enable measurements of ISM transverse motions in nearby clouds, opening a new window for studying ISM dynamics that is not accessible when using radial velocities alone.

papers.title: IXPE observation of the new magnetar source EP J223759.5+531421
papers.summary: We report on the detection of polarized X-ray emission from the new Galactic magnetar EP J223759.5+531421, discovered by the Einstein Probe Wide-field X-ray Telescope on 2026 June 28. The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) follow-up observation started on 2026 July 6 and detected the source at a (absorbed) flux of $\approx 4.5\times 10^{-11} \, \mathrm{ erg\,cm^2\,s}^{-1}$ ($2$--$7.5\, \mathrm{keV}$ range), confirming the presence of two thermally emitting regions on the star surface, with temperatures $\approx 0.5$ and $\approx 1\, \mathrm{keV}$. A significant (at $> 4\sigma$ confidence level) phase- and energy-integrated polarization degree of $\approx 7\%$ was detected with the polarization angle $\approx -2^\circ$ East of the celestial North. The two thermal components exhibit quite different polarization properties, with the hotter one being more polarized. The difference is larger in the phase-folded data, with the polarization degree reaching $\sim 63\%$ in the range $4$--$7.5\,\mathrm{keV}$, in correspondence with the secondary peak of the pulse profile, and never exceeding $\sim 30\%$ at lower energies. The polarization angle continuously oscillates from $-90^\circ$ to $+90^\circ$ over one rotational cycle and is well fit by the rotating vector model, with an inclination of the line of sight and of the magnetic dipole axis relative to the star spin axis of $\approx 28^\circ$ and $\approx 109^\circ$, respectively. The data point to an emission geometry in which the cold thermal component likely originates from two antipodal caps, possibly in a magnetically condensed state, while the hotter one comes from a smaller region covered by an atmosphere.

papers.title: The origin of the high heavy-element content of warm Jupiters
papers.summary: Planet interior models have revealed that warm Jupiters should harbor large heavy element masses (up to 30-40% of the planetary mass). Within the pebble drift and evaporation scenario, inward drifting pebbles can evaporate and enrich the inner disc with vapor to super-stellar values, accreteable by giant planets. As H$_2$O ice evaporates in the inner disc, while CO$_2$, CH$_4$ and CO evaporate in the outer disc, the enrichment of the disc with vapor decreases with increasing orbital distance. We use the chemcomp code to model the migration and growth of planets via pebble and gas accretion in discs around stars with different masses and discs with different sizes. We show (i) that pebble drift and evaporation can explain the wide range of derived heavy element contents of giant planets. (ii) Giant planets forming around stars with larger disc sizes can accrete larger quantities of heavy elements, because these discs can maintain a high pebble flux for a longer time. (iii) Planets forming or migrating interior to the water ice line can accrete larger amounts of heavy elements via the accretion of vapor enriched gas compared to planets forming in the outer disc regions. (iv) Metal rich stars can allow the formation of planets that are more enriched in heavy elements, if they form in the inner disc regions. Planets forming in the outer disc regions will be - independently of the disc metallicity - much less enriched compared. (v) Planets forming in discs with the same size and total mass, but around stars with higher mass, are only marginally more enriched compared to their counterparts forming around lower mass star. Our study suggests that the trend of increasing total heavy element mass with increasing planetary mass is caused by the accretion of vapor enriched gas in discs with different sizes in the combination with different origins of warm giant planets from the inner and outer disc.

papers.title: EMU detection of mysterious multiple component radio-continuum emission from nearby spiral Seyfert I type galaxy 'Sand-timer' (NGC 7213)
papers.summary: We present an Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) radio-continuum detection of the nearby spiral Seyfert I type galaxy NGC 7213 which we nickname `Sand-timer' due to its morphological appearance. We find intriguing, peculiar emission extending from the central supermassive black hole (SMBH), which we refer to as galaxy hyperbubbles and/or active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets. Finally, we find two previously undetected kiloparsec-scale features in the polarised intensity image, which appear most likely also related to the central SMBH, as restarted bipolar radio jets, though somewhat obscured in the radio-continuum total intensity image. They resemble the bow shocks often seen in Fanaroff-Riley Class II (FR-II) radio galaxies, and so we propose they most likely represent an early episode of the `Sand-timer's' AGN jet activity. An alternative scenario is that the core of NGC 7213 may be a supermassive binary black hole (SMBBH) undergoing a tidal disruption event (TDE), potentially causing the peculiar radio-continuum emission.

papers.title: Constrain the Size of Broad Line Region in NGC 1068 Using Sub-millimeter Excess
papers.summary: Constraining the size of broad-line region (BLR) close to the accretion disk in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is key to understand the central engine and evolution of AGN. We propose a new method to constrain the BLR size, based on millimeter to sub-millimeter spectral energy distribution (SED), from which a sub-millimeter excess may be found. Such excess can be used to determine the solid angle of the free-free emission region from BLR, as a region with high electron density and optically thick at sub-millimeter wavelength for free-free continuum. Millimeter to sub-millimeter SED analysis toward the central source S1 in a nearby type II AGN NGC 1068 was done, which gave an upper limit on the solid angle of BLR region as(4.94 +/- 0.61) *10^-6 arcsec^2, corresponding to a radius no more than 0.085 pc. Such a constraint on the BLR size is important for estimating the masses of central supermassive black holes in AGNs.

papers.title: Dark Matter in the Galaxy: Insights from the Dynamics of Stellar Streams
papers.summary: Dark matter constitutes most of the matter in the Universe, yet its fundamental nature and distribution remain poorly understood. Stellar streams, formed through the tidal disruption of globular clusters and dwarf galaxies, provide powerful tracers of the Milky Way's gravitational potential and dark matter halo. In this review, we examine how stellar stream morphology and kinematics can constrain the halo's structure, shape, and substructure. We discuss key observational signatures, including stream gaps, spurs, and perturbations, and investigate five prominent streams: Sagittarius, GD-1, Palomar 5, Orphan-Chenab, and Cetus Polar. We summarize analytical, statistical, and Bayesian methods used to model stellar streams and infer dark matter properties, highlighting challenges arising from parameter degeneracies, incomplete observations, progenitor uncertainties, and time-dependent perturbations, particularly those associated with the Large Magellanic Cloud. Finally, we discuss how upcoming astrometric and photometric surveys, together with improved dynamical modelling, may strengthen constraints on the Milky Way's dark matter distribution and help distinguish between cold, warm, and self-interacting dark matter scenarios.

papers.title: Chemical Demographics of Star-forming Regions
papers.summary: Our understanding of complex organic chemistry during the formation of stars and planets is shaped by a handful of cherry-picked sources with bright molecular emission lines. This observational bias impedes our assessment of how universal chemical complexity is during star formation. The lack of systematic wideband spectral surveys for statistically significant samples of protostars and cores is a major roadblock to properly probing how COM inventories and abundances depend on the vast range of physical conditions, local cloud and global galactic environments, and evolutionary timescales of low- and high-mass star formation. In turn, this limits our ability to constrain and test physicochemical models, which depend critically on these parameters. The next-generation ALMA2040, with a 10x improvement in line sensitivity, is required to observe COMs, that we perceive as common today, in a fraction of the observing time that is needed today with ALMA. Such capabilities will propel us into the era of chemical demographics, whereby wideband (>100 GHz) spectral surveys at high sensitivity (routinely probing COM abundances down to 0.01% relative to CH3OH) will be executed towards >1000-10000 prestellar and protostellar sources. With robust chemical inventories towards large source sample sizes, we will be able to probe for dependencies of chemical complexity on mass regime, feedback processes in a cluster, Galactic position, metallicity, and time-variable accretion. Only with statistically significant samples at high sensitivity will we be able to assess the ubiquity and homogeneity of COM chemistry across the protostellar mass spectrum and natal cores. Constraining the diversity and availability of such species is critical for our understanding of the chemical reservoir available for planet formation, which eventually shapes (exo)planetary atmosphere compositions.

papers.title: Scattered light noise due to dust particles contamination in the vacuum pipes of the Einstein Telescope
papers.summary: High-sensitivity optical measurements such as those performed in interferometric gravitational wave detectors are prone to scattered light noise. To minimize it, optical components must meet tight requirements on surface roughness and bulk defects. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of these measures can be undermined by other sources of scattered light. In this article, we examine scattered light noise caused by particles deposited on surfaces, especially on the baffles inside the vacuum pipes of the Einstein Telescope's interferometer arms. First, we study light scattering by particles deposited on a surface and having diameters from about one tenth to hundred times the light wavelength: we discuss its angular distribution and dependence on particle size and refractive index, and on polarization. Then, we specialize to the case of the Einstein Telescope arms and quantify the maximum allowed density of particles on each arm baffle. We conclude with cleanliness guidelines for the assembly of the vacuum pipes, including the required cleanliness class of the installation environment.

papers.title: Cracking Gravitational Wave Multiple Ringdown Modes in Space
papers.summary: Ringdown signals from perturbed black holes (BHs) offer a clean window into BH spacetime, strong-field gravity, and fundamental physics. Presently the quasi-normal modes of stellar-mass BH ringdowns have been successfully extracted in the ground-based gravitational wave (GW) observations. Looking ahead, the future space-borne observatories will listen to the ringdowns from massive BH binary coalescences more loudly and resolve multiple modes to unprecedented precision, which calls for efficient approaches to mitigate the sharply increasing computational burden. We develop a practical ringdown analysis pipeline for space-borne detectors by implementing FIREFLY, a novel acceleration algorithm validated in ground-based detectors, and for the first time demonstrate its compatibility and effectiveness with the time-delay interferometry (TDI) observables. With high fidelity, we achieve an over two-order-of-magnitude speedup for a simulated ringdown signal including six modes, providing a viable and scalable route for multi-mode ringdown analysis in the space context. This new approach has sound statistical interpretation and is extensible to other GW sources in band.

papers.title: Evolutionary Informed Translation from Protein to Nucleic Acid Sequence
papers.summary: The choice of nucleic acid sequence for a given protein strongly impacts function and is species-specific. Current protein-to-nucleic-acid translation models treat sequences in isolation, often over-favoring frequently used codons. To generate more natural nucleic acid sequences, we introduce PINATA (Phylogenetically Informed protein to Nucleic Acid Translation with sequence Alignment), a model that leverages sequences from related species encoded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to guide prediction. Our architecture leverages evolutionary context and learns species-and protein specific context to make biologically-informed predictions. Evaluated across 61,934 gene trees and 882 species, PINATA generates sequences that mirror the naturally-occurring sequence substantially better than existing language models. PINATA leverages MSA data to improve exact native codon recovery by 17.95 percentage points over existing language models, effectively preserves natural rare-codon nuances, and more closely matches native sequence properties. PINATA maintains strong predictive performance even with limited evolutionary data. While previous methods largely treated sequences from different species in isolation, our method leverages the evolutionary relationships between nucleic acids and proteins across species to create a more biologically-informed translation. We demonstrate that leveraging rich evolutionary data through an biologically-designed method strongly aids in translating protein sequences to nucleic acid sequences across species. We will make data and code publicly available upon publication.

papers.title: Harness-Driven Agentic Operation of Optical Pooled Screen Analysis
papers.summary: Optical pooled screens connect genetic perturbations to changes in cell morphology and behavior, but turning the microscopy data into interpretable results takes complex, multi-day analyses. Established pipelines process this data, yet researchers still select parameters, inspect outputs, and resolve failures for each experiment. Here, we present Brieflow-auto, a pipeline-specific harness implemented as a Claude Code plugin that lets a coding large language model (LLM) operate Brieflow, an open-source end-to-end pipeline for optical pooled screening data. A researcher supplies experimental facts and approves the launch. An agent tunes parameters in an interactive notebook, and the harness validates the configuration, monitors execution, recovers from common failures, and checks output quality. For pipeline defects, the agent opens upstream issues proposing backward-compatible fixes for the broader community. In five previously analyzed screens, harness runs yielded more cells with a confident single-gene assignment than the original hand analyses. On a screen the pipeline was not designed for, the harness turned each failure into a reviewed upstream fix. More broadly, we propose that wrapping an established pipeline in a harness can substantially accelerate its use and the long-term reliability of its codebase.

papers.title: Amplifying gene expression sensitivity by surface condensation on DNA
papers.summary: Condensation of proteins on DNA is a central aspect of genome organisation, and has been proposed as a mechanism of gene regulation in eukaryotes, notably by mediating the action of distal enhancers on promoter activity. However, the physics of this interaction and its impact on the precision of gene regulation remain to be fully elucidated. Here, we study a simplified system of two regulatory regions of the DNA, a distal enhancer and a promoter, with affinity to a self-attracting ligand that effectively binds them together. Using 3-dimensional lattice simulations and a mean-field theory of the ligand-water mixture coupled to a Rouse polymer, we show that small differences in ligand concentrations can be greatly amplified at the level of transcriptional activity compared to a free ligand receptor. We quantify this sensitivity using the Fisher information rate, which can be decomposed into two contributions. First, the formation of a pre-wet layer of ligands around regulatory regions increases ligand concentrations at the promoter site, enhancing concentration differences. Second, the DNA polymer itself switches between a closed state, where enhancer and promoter are in contact through an attractive capillary bridge formed by ligands, and an open state where they are apart. That attractive force determines the typical dwell time of the closed configuration where the gene is most active, and strongly depends on the ligand bulk concentration, contributing to the sensitivity of gene expression. These results suggest a general mechanism and theoretical framework for the precise regulation of genes through tunable genome organization.

papers.title: MultiPASE: Shape-Aware Comparative 3D Genome Analysis
papers.summary: 3D genome structures reconstructed from Hi-C data provide valuable insights into chromatin organization, but comparing them across conditions and time points remains challenging because of noise, variability, and arbitrary orientation. State-of-the-art comparison approaches often rely on contact-matrix-based summaries, which do not preserve the spatial geometry of the reconstructed structures and make integration with gene expression and chromatin accessibility difficult. There is therefore a need for robust structural alignment and spatial abstraction methods that support integrated analysis across conditions and time points. We present MultiPASE, a computational pipeline for comparative analysis of reconstructed 3D genome structures represented as gene-level spatial point clouds. MultiPASE aligns point clouds into a shared coordinate frame using coarse-to-fine rigid registration with PCA-based axis disambiguation and robust ICP refinement, then summarizes spatial organization using two complementary shape abstraction methods that produce stable, nested, multi-scale representations from dense core regions to broader structural extent. Using Hi-C-derived reconstructions from viral infection experiments, we show how the approach reveals condition-dependent structural changes that are difficult to interpret from raw 3D structures alone. By integrating spatial structure with gene expression and chromatin accessibility, MultiPASE supports interactive analysis of spatial organization and gene relocation patterns. A quantitative validation, reported in the Supplementary Materials, shows that the proposed shape abstractions preserve non-convex features, remain stable across samples, and that the alignment pipeline is necessary for meaningful comparison. A usage case and a usability evaluation with eight participants demonstrate the pipeline's effectiveness for comparative structural analysis.

papers.title: Molecular genetics of Aedes aegypti: historical advances and oversights
papers.summary: The yellow fever mosquito Aedes aegypti has a rich history of molecular genetic work but in recent years this has lagged behind rivals such as Anopheles, owing to the nature of control efforts focused on Ae. aegypti and the complex structure of its genome. However, Ae. aegypti has now entered the whole-genomic era of molecular genetics, with many whole genome sequences of individuals now publicly available for analysis. These resources enable an unprecedented view on several core genetic questions that have vexed research on the species for decades. They also create the possibility for new genomic analyses to be developed in the future. In this review, we consider the history of molecular genetic technology as it applies to Ae. aegypti, with a special emphasis on how emerging pictures of the genome both enabled and in some cases constrained the development of work on population genetics and insecticide resistance. We integrate historical and contemporary perspectives to diagnose gaps and biases within the Ae. aegypti literature that require further clarification and research. In particular, these highlight underrepresentation of the Indo-Pacific region in whole genome datasets relative to its dengue burden, and the overlooking of copy number variation in resistance studies owing to difficulties of sequence alignment in duplicated regions, particularly around the glutathione S-transferase epsilon class of genes.

papers.title: Multiscale Quantum-Classical Simulation of Protein Autoproteolysis in a Million-Atom Membrane Environment
papers.summary: Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.

papers.title: EEG Lempel-Ziv Complexity vis-\`a-vis Autocorrelation Function
papers.summary: Measures of signal complexity have become increasingly popular in electroencephalography (EEG), where they are often interpreted as indicators of neural information processing, dynamical richness, or conscious state. In contrast, classical measures of temporal dependence, such as the autocorrelation function (ACF), remain more directly linked to known physiological mechanisms and are easier to interpret. The present work revisits, for the EEG practicioner, the relation between normalized Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZC) and temporal autocorrelation in both synthetic and physiological EEG signals. First, synthetic time series exhibiting a broad range of temporal structure and complexity levels were generated using stochastic processes with varying degrees of temporal dependence. LZC and autocorrelation measures were then computed and compared. Across simulated signals, a robust inverse relationship was observed between normalized LZC and the first autocorrelation coefficient, indicating that signals with stronger temporal correlations exhibit lower complexity estimates. This relationship also holds in resting-state EEG recordings from healthy adult participants across channels and subjects, as well as dynamically during eyes open/close maneuvers. Overall, these results show that the information captured by LZC reflects temporal redundancy already quantified by conventional autocorrelation measures. Because autocorrelation measures relate more directly to established neurophysiological mechanisms, including oscillatory persistence, network synchronization, and temporal integration, these results suggest that interpreting complexity-based EEG findings should explicitly account for their dependence on conventional temporal statistics, which may provide a more transparent framework for mechanistic inferences.

papers.title: The nearest neighbor interchange proximity measure for the tree-basedness of rooted binary phylogenetic networks
papers.summary: Tree-based networks are a broad graph class in phylogenetics which posit a model of evolution composed of tree-like processes and hybridization events. Hence, for any non-tree-based phylogenetic network, it is meaningful to study the magnitude of violation of the tree-based model assumptions. For rooted networks, we introduce the proximity measure delta_rNNI, defined by the minimum number of rooted nearest neighbor interchanges (NNIs) required to transform a network into a tree-based network. For binary networks, we prove that delta_rNNI is pairwise distinct from all previously known proximity measures in the literature and that no approximation guarantees between delta_rNNI and other known proximity measures holds. In addition, we characterize a family of networks for which a linear time lower bound on delta_rNNI is tight. Moreover, we analyze upper bounds and give an exact solution algorithm to compute delta_rNNI.

papers.title: Multiplayer games on regular graphs under aspiration-driven imitation: Fixation probabilities and the dilution principle
papers.summary: We investigate how cooperation evolves in multiplayer games on regular graphs of degree $k$ when individuals base their decisions on both their own aspiration levels and the success of their neighbors. We calculate explicit first-order formulas for fixation probabilities using pair approximation and diffusion methods under weak selection. These formulas separate aspiration effects from payoff effects filtered by the graph. We show that increasing the graph degree attenuates the selection effects driven by payoffs. In contrast, the contribution of the aspiration gap $\Delta\alpha=\alpha_D-\alpha_C$ is independent of graph degree at first order. We apply the framework to public goods, stag-hunt, and snowdrift games and obtain corresponding conditions for the evolutionary success of cooperation. In the public goods and stag-hunt games, the conditions at large degree retain cost terms, so cooperation requires a sufficiently positive aspiration gap to compensate for the cost of contributing. In the snowdrift game, both benefit and cost contributions vanish in the locally tree-like regime at large degree, leaving the aspiration gap as the leading first-order contribution. Monte Carlo simulations on connected random regular graphs of degree $k$ are consistent with the first-order predictions within their formal regime of validity, while simulations outside this regime are interpreted only as qualitative checks of the predicted trends.

papers.title: Heterogeneity among and competition between life stages together extend the stability boundary of complex ecological communities
papers.summary: Classical models of pairwise species interactions consistently predict that large, complex communities are inherently unstable, yet the observed persistence of diverse communities highlights a central contradiction in theoretical ecology. While foundational frameworks often model species as homogeneous populations, one theoretical resolution lies in including internal species structure. In this work, we incorporate explicit demographic stage structure into a generalized Lotka-Volterra framework to evaluate how ontogenetic changes throughout the life cycle of a species can affect whole-community stability. We show that stage-dependence of inter-specific interactions can significantly expand the stable parameter space for a species network. Furthermore, this enhanced stability requires strong competition between life stages of a species. Our study illustrates that stage structure with population heterogeneity expands classical stability criteria, providing a mathematical foundation for understanding how ontogeny modifies the classically derived complexity boundaries for local asymptotic stability.

papers.title: Causal Integrated Gradients: Scalable Feature Attribution Along Causal Paths
papers.summary: Existing feature attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions. We propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), which extend integrated gradients to incorporate prior causal structure among input features while retaining its computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, its axiomatic guarantees. In many settings, some causal structure between features is already known, for example, that a transcription factor causally regulates a target gene's expression. Yet existing gradient-based methods cannot exploit this structure, instead crediting a feature's downstream effects over its true upstream cause, such as ranking the target gene above the transcription factor that regulates it. Our key idea is to embed this causal structure by routing the integration path along the causal graph. The method thereby decomposes each feature's attribution into a direct effect and effects mediated through its causal descendants. We evaluate CIG in three settings of increasing realism. First, on a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, CIG's attributions best match the ground-truth causal effect from Pearl's do-calculus, matching the accuracy of causal Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Second, on simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon-$\beta$ stimulation data, where only an approximate causal graph is available, CIG better prioritizes the transcription factors driving the measured response than DeepSHAP and integrated gradients. Together, these results show that incorporating causal structure into gradient-based attributions recovers upstream drivers that existing methods miss, without sacrificing scalability.

papers.title: napari-TurboBox: Interactive Multi-Viewer Bounding Box Annotation for AI-Guided Volumetric Bioimaging
papers.summary: Promptable segmentation models turn one 3D bounding box into an instance mask. Box placement therefore limits how fast microscopy volumes with thousands of objects are annotated. Each box must be checked in several synchronized viewers, but napari-bbox shares no state between viewers. An edit must update every viewer and slows down with more boxes. napari-TurboBox instead holds one shared copy of the boxes for all viewers. In a four-viewer layout, napari-TurboBox needs a few milliseconds per mouse move to update the three slice viewers up to $10^4$ boxes. The same update in napari-bbox leaves the 33 ms budget beyond about $10^3$ boxes and takes 159 ms at $10^4$. Boxes stay axis-aligned and export to COCO and YOLO as per-slice 2D boxes. napari-TurboBox is a pure-Python plugin for napari 0.6.6 to 0.9. The code is available at https://github.com/N-Friederich/napari-turbobox under the Apache 2.0 licence, and version 0.1.0 is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23090828 on Zenodo.

papers.title: Brain-Aligned Multimodal LLMs for Social and Emotional Understanding of Cartoon Movies
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer scalable annotations of social and affective content, but their temporal agreement with human judgments and neural predictive value require further evaluation. We compared diffusion-based and autoregressive MLLMs with continuous human Theory of Mind (ToM) and affective valence ratings across three short cartoon movies. Behavioral analyses assessed temporally aligned Pearson correlations, rating distributions, and the effects of preceding scene descriptions. Ratings from each source were separately used in subject-specific regression models to predict regional fMRI responses. Model ratings captured aspects of human temporal variation despite systematic distributional differences, with generally stronger alignment for valence than ToM. Preceding context improved alignment in some conditions, depending on the model and movie. In \emph{The Present}, more regions showed significant encoding for MLLM ratings than for human ratings, whereas effects were more limited in the other movies. Spatial overlap across rating sources occurred mainly among MLLMs; overlap between human and model ratings was limited and involved primarily visual, dorsal-attention, and posterior default-mode regions. These findings support MLLMs as scalable tools for generating brain-predictive annotations of social and emotional content, while highlighting systematic rating differences and model- and stimulus-dependent alignment with human judgments.

papers.title: Image Moment Estimation for Crowded Datasets
papers.summary: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is an imaging technique capable of reconstructing high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) structure of biological macromolecules from a set of noisy projection images taken at random viewing directions. The mathematical model for cryo-EM images typically assumes that each image contains exactly one particle, which is centered at the origin. However, many experimental datasets contain particle images which include multiple particles: one central particle and a few crowding particles. This deviation from the model leads to inaccurate estimation of image statistics, such as the low-order image moments. To account for this, we propose a method to estimate image moments while correcting for the effect of crowding particles. This method can be run directly from a set of cryo-EM micrographs with picked particles, and we demonstrate its efficacy on a wide array of synthetic data.

papers.title: Nondimensionalization, Variational Inequalities and Uncertainty Quantification in a Morphoelastic Model for Burn Injury Healing
papers.summary: Mathematical modelling of burn injury healing involves coupling biological processes with mechanical deformation, resulting in computationally stiff, nonlinear partial differential equations that severely limit the scalability of existing numerical solutions. We present a computational framework addressing these challenges. By nondimensionalizing the model and performing scaling analysis, we show that chemotaxis and inertia are negligible, permitting a quasi-static momentum approach. To enforce non-negativity constraints, we implement a Variational Inequality formulation using the Finite Element Method in FEniCSx, and verify it via numerical convergence studies and mass balances. We identify high-order parameter interactions, specifically equilibrium collagen density and signalling dynamics, as the primary drivers of solver stability. A sensitivity analysis of nearly four million simulations reveals that isolated parameter variations predominantly govern the maximum wound contraction. In contrast, higher-order interactions determine the timing of maximum contraction and the permanent contracture. However, no significant pairwise parameter interactions were found, suggesting that the model's behaviour is governed by higher-order interactions, highlighting the inherent complexity of the wound-healing process.

papers.title: Fundamental Bounds on the Oscillation Efficiency of Markov Networks
papers.summary: Stochastic oscillations are commonly identified through peaks in their power spectra, yet the fundamental limits on their strength and energetic cost remain unclear. Here we establish universal dynamical and thermodynamic bounds on oscillation efficiency in Markov networks, showing how finite state spaces constrain spectral peak enhancement. In particular, we demonstrate that networks maximizing modal coherence need not maximize oscillation efficiency. We further derive dissipation bounds that connect oscillation efficiency to the relaxation speed and stationary probabilities, revealing an unavoidable energetic cost of maintaining pronounced oscillations at a specified relaxation timescale. These bounds remain strictly positive in regimes where existing explicit spectral dissipation estimates vanish, with stronger constraints for normal networks and uniform rings. Our results distinguish spectral oscillatory strength from modal coherence and reveal how network dynamics and thermodynamic dissipation jointly limit stochastic oscillations.

papers.title: Effect of an auditory static distractor on the perception of an auditory moving target
papers.summary: It is known that listeners lose the ability to discriminate the direction of motion of a revolving sound (clockwise vs counterclockwise) beyond a critical velocity ["the upper limit (UL)"], likely due to degraded front-back discrimination. Little is known about how this ability is affected by simultaneously present distractor sounds, despite the real-life importance of tracking moving sounds in the presence of distractors. We hypothesized that the presence of a static distractor sound would impair the perception of moving target sounds and reduce the UL and show that this is indeed the case. A distractor on the right was as effective as a distractor at the front in reducing the UL, despite the likely importance of resolving front-back confusions. By manipulating the spectral content of both the target and distractor, we found that the UL was significantly reduced only when the distractor spectrally overlaps with the target in the frequency range relevant for front-back discrimination. Our findings form the first steps toward a better understanding of the tracking of multiple sounds in the presence of distractors.

papers.title: Inter- and Intra-Subject Variability in EEG: A Systematic Survey
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) underpins neuroscience, clinical neurophysiology, and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), yet pronounced inter- and intra-subject variability limits reliability, reproducibility, and translation. This systematic review studies that quantified or modeled EEG variability across resting-state, event-related potentials (ERPs), and task-related/BCI paradigms (including motor imagery and SSVEP) in healthy and clinical cohorts. Across paradigms, inter-subject differences are typically larger than within-subject fluctuations, but both affect inference and model generalization. Stability is feature-dependent: alpha-band measures and individual alpha peak frequency are often relatively reliable, whereas higher-frequency and many connectivity-derived metrics show more heterogeneous reliability; ERP reliability varies by component, with P300 measures frequently showing moderate-to-good stability. We summarize major sources of variability (biological, state-related, technical, and analytical), review common quantification and modeling approaches (e.g., ICC, CV, SNR, generalizability theory, and multivariate/learning-based methods), and provide recommendations for study design, reporting, and harmonization. Overall, EEG variability should be treated as both a practical constraint to manage and a meaningful signal to leverage for precision neuroscience and robust neurotechnology.

papers.title: Effect of antibiotic spectrum on the abundance of resistant bacteria in multispecies communities
papers.summary: Antibiotic resistance is a major threat to global health. It emerges in multispecies microbial communities under antibiotic exposure. This makes antibiotic spectrum --- a drug's distribution of effects across species --- a potential key parameter in resistance management. However, current theory for resistance dynamics is not well-developed for the effect of antibiotics in a multispecies setting. Analysing a well-established model in community ecology theory --- the generalized Lotka-Volterra model --- we develop a simple mathematical measure for how an antibiotic effect on one taxon (strain or species) affects another taxon through all direct and indirect interactions in a complex interaction network. Using this measure, we predict the expected effects of different antibiotic spectra on the abundance of resistant taxa in microbial communities. This furthers our understanding of the community ecology of antibiotic resistance, and provides a formal theoretical basis for empirical work on optimal antibiotic choice.

papers.title: From anatomy to computation: axonal delay dispersion shifts neurons from event to sequence detection
papers.summary: Cortical neurons fire sparsely -- often fewer than one spike per sensory window -- so a neuron's spike count in that window carries little information, and its spike timing can carry more. That conduction delays convert firing order into synchrony is long established. What governs which class of temporal feature a neuron detects -- one volley of coincident input, or two in a particular order -- has not been examined. We propose a delay-signature framework in which the axonal conduction delays converging on a dendritic branch or a small neuron's soma constitute a physical key: only input sequences whose spike-time differences the delays compensate arrive synchronously, and coincidence detection, a threshold on input summed within an inhibition-compressed window, converts that synchrony into an all-or-none output. First, in simulations of an integrator-neuron model, a single physical scalar -- the dispersion of the delay set -- moves a population from event to order-selective sequence detection. The transition is emergent under random delays and connectivity, and an exact calculation reproduces it: at narrow dispersion, sequence detectors do not exist, and the dispersion at which they overtake event detectors tracks the inter-event interval. This maps a computational distinction onto the anatomical one between myelinated and unmyelinated projections, making myelination a switch on what a neuron computes. Second, the same dispersion sets the code's limits: it bounds the longest codable interval and fixes an absolute timing tolerance of order a millisecond, the same at every dispersion. Third, that millisecond window and the conduction velocity of afferents inside cortex together set column diameter, and column anatomy predicts the window measured in mouse barrel cortex. One anatomically measurable parameter thus shapes what a neuron detects and sets the limits of what it can represent.

papers.title: Covariance Eigenspace Provides Latent Attribution of Longitudinal Effects in Brain Age Gap
papers.summary: Brain age gap is a promising machine learning (ML)-driven bio\-marker of accelerated biological aging and is derived from neuroimaging data. Recent works on coVariance neural networks (VNN) for brain age gap prediction have provided an explainable and anatomically verifiable framework for brain age gap prediction. Notably, VNN outcomes are derived by filtering inputs along covariance eigenvectors, providing a mechanism for explaining their decisions in terms of latent (orthogonal) vectors. In this paper, we investigate the longitudinal brain age gap effects in a Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) cohort using a VNN-driven brain age gap prediction framework. Specifically, using Integrated Gradients (IG) as the attribution mechanism, our results demonstrate that the eigenspectrum of the anatomical covariance matrix explains the different longitudinal effects observed in brain age gap in amyloid positive vs amyloid negative subcohorts more prominently than individual brain regions ($83.2\%$ with the leading eigenvector versus a maximal value of $7.7\%$ for any brain region). Therefore, the covariance-based latent explanation identifies a key coordinated input pattern that carries most of the observed longitudinal effect in brain age gap.

papers.title: Computing Extinction Barriers in a Quorum-Sensing Reaction Network
papers.summary: We introduce a simple reaction-network model of a quorum-sensing population that couples the cell density $x$ to the signal density $w$. In the four-channel cell-signal network studied here, scaling signal production and removal by the same factor $r$ leaves all deterministic equilibria, and their stability types, unchanged. Nevertheless, we show that $r$ shifts the quasipotential barrier $\Delta V(r)$ for rare transitions towards extinction, and thus, under metastable exit assumptions, the mean time to reach a fixed neighbourhood of the extinction state on the exponential scale $e^{N\Delta V(r)}$. We compute the barrier by minimization of the path action with the signal retained as a fluctuating coordinate, and we check it against mean extinction times obtained without the action solver, i.e., from the backward equation of the jump process on a truncated lattice and from exact stochastic simulation. Over a range of $r$, the minimum-action barriers satisfy $\Delta V(r)=\Delta V_\infty+O(1/r)$, where $\Delta V_\infty$ is obtained by eliminating the signal first, and at $r=1$ the barrier is 55% larger than $\Delta V_\infty$. A formal first-order expansion attributes this increase to the lag of the signal, of which the fluctuations of the signal remove a quarter. The saddle barrier $\Delta V(r)$ is also the least action needed to enter the basin of extinction, whereas the density threshold can be crossed more cheaply, by paths which keep the signal high and are usually followed by recovery. The mean extinction times of the backward equation, which include failed attempts, have a prefactor which tends to a constant, and they grow at a rate within $10^{-5}$ of $\Delta V(r)$ at every tested rate.

papers.title: Typical Superpositions are Magical
papers.summary: The non-stabilizerness, or "magic", of a quantum state is a common metric for the hardness of simulation on a classical computer, and is often quantified by the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy (SRE). We show how random superpositions of classically simulable states saturate the SRE to the symmetry-restricted Haar-random maximum. For any large-$N$ random pure-state ensemble satisfying the conditions of Schur's lemma, the average SRE of the $m$-component superposition $\langle M_2(m)\rangle=N-\log_2[\langle W(m)\rangle]$ is governed by an average witness $\langle W(m)\rangle$ that universally decomposes into a Haar floor and an ensemble-specific excess. As the number of components $m$ increases, the excess is suppressed, resulting in a logarithmic scaling of the SRE before plateauing at the Haar-valued maximum. We derive a general closed form for $\langle W(m)\rangle$ in the thermodynamic limit, and numerically verify our result for random stabilizer states and random Gaussian states.

papers.title: Exploring Quantum Phase Transitions Beyond Landau Theory on a Quantum Processor
papers.summary: Direct continuous quantum phase transitions between phases that break distinct symmetries challenge the conventional Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm and provide a framework for deconfined quantum criticality. Here, we investigate a Landau-forbidden ferromagnetic-to-valence-bond-solid (FM-VBS) transition in a frustrated one-dimensional spin chain using superconducting quantum processors. Combining matrix-product-state-assisted circuit preparation with quantum-hardware measurements, we resolve the suppression of long-range ferromagnetic correlations and the redistribution of competing-order fluctuations across the transition. Distance-resolved correlations and finite-size analyses reveal signatures consistent with critical behavior. We further extend our investigation to nonequilibrium dynamics, directly preparing dimerized states and tracking the evolution of VBS order and joint FM-VBS fluctuations under local unitary interactions. Our results establish a versatile quantum-hardware framework for probing competing orders, critical correlations, and many-body dynamics beyond conventional Landau theory.

papers.title: Multi-Time States in Quantum and Operational Probabilistic Theories: An Axiomatic Framework
papers.summary: Quantum states over time were introduced, in part, to extend Bayesian probability to quantum theory and have since found applications across diverse areas, ranging from quantum causality and open-system dynamics to tests of macroscopic realism. While axiomatic characterizations of these states exist for Markovian dynamics, a general framework accommodating non-Markovian dynamics is still lacking. Moreover, extending this framework beyond quantum mechanics to general physical theories also remains elusive. In this work, we develop an axiomatic framework for multi-time states within a class of operational probabilistic theories (OPTs) that includes quantum mechanics as a special case. Based on three assumptions---compositionality, reconstructibility, and spatio-temporal marginal consistency---the framework accommodates both Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics, and provides sufficient conditions to certify signaling and temporal memory within OPT. As a concrete application of our OPT framework, we fully characterize the unique multi-time state in boxworld and develop a method for Bayesian retrodiction of physical transformations there. Our general framework is consistent with quantum theory, reproducing several existing results. In the non-Markovian quantum dynamics, we establish a correspondence between multi-time states and the process-matrix framework, and fully characterize the multi-time states compatible with general dynamics. This correspondence also lets us infer quantum causal models from multi-time states, and as a proof of principle, we propose a semidefinite program to infer causal order from quantum multi-time states. These results provide a unified framework for studying spatio-temporal states, causal relations, and Bayesian reasoning within OPTs, with implications for both fundamental and applied research.

papers.title: Circuit Synthesis for Variational Quantum Algorithms: The Depth of Algebra and Geometry
papers.summary: The analysis of Hamiltonian Variational Ans\"atze centers on three fundamental questions: which states are exactly reachable from a given initial state, what native control depth suffices for local and global synthesis, and whether a bounded circuit extension can expose a direction of decreasing cost at a suboptimal output. We address these challenges by leveraging the dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) associated with the circuits and the geometry of the initial state's orbit under the action of the corresponding dynamical Lie group $G$. We show that an initial state has a closed projective orbit whenever it is a nondegenerate eigenstate of a control Hamiltonian. Combined with asymptotic QAOA convergence, this guarantees exact, finite depth ground state preparation for architectures employing diagonal problem Hamiltonians and irreducible stoquastic mixers. We bound the number of native control exponentials required for local unitary synthesis and state preparation using DLA commutator filtration growth alongside reachable orbit dimensions. Complementing these local results, we construct global frameworks on invariant sectors equipped with full unitary or special unitary dynamical Lie algebras. These constructions yield explicit applications to Pauli-generated systems and constrained maximum independent set multi-angle QAOA circuits; specifically, we show that their native control costs are directly determined by commutator filtration depth and independent-set toggle-group geometry, respectively. Finally, if the dynamical Lie group is compact, the observable $H_P$ generates an admissible evolution ($iH_P \in \mathfrak{g}$, where $\mathfrak{g}$ is the DLA), and the projective orbit of the initial state contains a ground state ray of $H_P$, then a bounded depth, identity-initialized circuit extension exhibits either first-order descent or negative curvature at every suboptimal circuit output.
