papers.title: Caustics and catastrophes in strong-field physics $-$ Picard-Lefschetz theory as a universal approach to saddle-point methods in attosecond science
papers.summary: Ultrashort laser pulses on the attosecond timescale are typically achieved via high-order harmonic generation (HHG), a nonlinear process in which atoms interact with intense light fields to emit a broad spectrum of harmonics. HHG is commonly described in terms of a `quantum orbits' model based on several interfering electron trajectories, thereby incorporating both quantum-mechanical effects and an intuitive picture of classical dynamics. By tuning the parameters of the driving laser field, the interplay between these trajectories can be controlled, shaping the emitted light. Mathematically, this model expresses the harmonic response as a highly oscillatory integral. Applying saddle-point methods to this integral allows it to be decomposed into contributions from distinct saddle points of the semi-classical action, thereby linking quantum dynamics to classical trajectories. However, a general framework for applying these methods across arbitrary parameters and laser configurations has been missing. In this thesis, we introduce Picard-Lefschetz theory and develop practical numerical methods for its application. These enable the evaluation of oscillatory integrals and identification of contributions from individual critical points. We apply these techniques to strong-field ionisation and HHG, focusing on caustics $-$ enhancement features where trajectories coalesce and standard approximations fail. Our methods remain valid in these regions, allowing systematic analysis of parameter regimes and revealing previously inaccessible features. This work improves the understanding and control of ultrafast light-matter interactions.

papers.title: A finite-shot mean-squared-error boundary for Richardson zero-noise extrapolation
papers.summary: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) reduces the bias of noisy quantum-circuit measurements, but Richardson coefficients and shot splitting increase their statistical error. This paper determines the noise strength at which Richardson ZNE starts to lower the mean-squared error relative to the unmitigated estimator at a fixed shot budget $B$. The boundary is set by the balance between the leading squared-bias improvement and the leading excess-variance penalty: depending on the variance exponent of the measurement, it shrinks with $B$, becomes a budget threshold, or disappears. For fixed Richardson extrapolation with linear leading bias, the Richardson order and the shot allocation change only constants; the boundary exponent is set by the measured observable and protocol. Deterministic stabilizer measurements and nonzero-variance Hamiltonian or variational-energy measurements have boundaries that shrink as $B^{-1}$ and $B^{-1/2}$, and for finite-outcome shot measurements these two classes are the only ones. Qiskit Aer simulations of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) circuits reproduce this separation, and on IBM Quantum hardware ZNE lowers the mean-squared error at equal budget in 75 of 101 instances.

papers.title: Learning Midcircuit Measurement Backaction from Three Repeated Measurements
papers.summary: Accurate modeling of midcircuit measurements (MCMs) is essential for dynamic-circuit operations such as syndrome extraction, measurement-based reset, and the separation of state-preparation and measurement error. Unlike terminal measurement, a noisy MCM both produces a classical outcome and alters the incoming quantum state, thereby influencing subsequent circuit operations. This makes conventional confusion-matrix or fidelity-level characterization insufficient. Here, we introduce an efficient, self-consistent protocol for learning a single-qubit Z-twirled MCM instrument, retaining the readout-backaction correlations and excitation-decay asymmetry that are erased in Pauli-error descriptions. Remarkably, readout bit strings from only three repeated MCMs on a maximally mixed input determine all learnable parameters of the reduced instrument, up to a single unidentifiable gauge degree of freedom. Physicality constraints convert this nonidentifiability into narrow, gauge-aware error intervals. Implemented on IBM superconducting processors, the learned instrument improves Pauli-observable prediction by $\sim 100\times$ over a conventional confusion-matrix model and reveals a $T_1$-decay dominated backaction. Our protocol provides a compact characterization layer for state-preparation and measurement error separation, reset optimization, and noise-aware quantum error correction.

papers.title: Spectral theory of energy-selective quantum search with Ising Hamiltonian phase oracles
papers.summary: We develop an exact spectral-response theory for the Grover-type iterate \(W_T=D_\xi\exp(-\mathrm{i} T H)\), in which the evolution generated by a diagonal Ising Hamiltonian is used directly as a continuous phase oracle. An energy-grouped recurrence and its generating-function solution show how the empirical characteristic function determines the position, width, height, and saturation time of an energy-selective resonance. For an annealed Gaussian density of states, a high-density-tail resonance containing \(M\) configurations is reached after \(\Theta(\sqrt{2^n/M})\) oracle calls with success probability \(\Theta(1)\), giving a quadratic query improvement over independent uniform sampling with classical energy evaluation. For correlated random Ising spectra, overlap-dependent covariances lead to a realization-dependent resonance shift with root-mean-square scale \(O(n^{-3})\), parametrically larger than the resonance width, and can also reduce the peak height. The shift is both an algorithmic detuning and a coherent probe of sample-specific spectral fluctuations whose ensemble statistics reflect the Ising overlap structure. Spectral symmetrization and iterative calibration can remove or compensate the resonance-center displacement for prescribed-energy targeting. We also clarify the relation to designed spectral filters and the precision and coherence requirements of this asymptotic primitive.

papers.title: Dominant Eigenstate Isolation through Symmetry-Orbit Decoupling
papers.summary: We address the problem of extracting a target eigenstate from an approximate pure state. Our approach, symmetry-orbit decoupling, exploits symmetries that preserve the target state while acting differently on the residual. Averaging over the resulting orbit suppresses the target--residual coherence without reducing the target population, thereby exposing a spectral structure that is hidden in the original pure state. When the target is sufficiently separated from the residual modes, it becomes the principal mode of the orbit-averaged state and can be identified through the orbit Gram matrix. Numerical VQE simulations performed with QuESTlink for six- and eight-qubit Heisenberg and Fermi--Hubbard chains show substantial improvements in ground-state energy estimation. The remaining accuracy is limited by residual components that are indistinguishable from the target under the chosen symmetry.

papers.title: Enhancing Quantum Metrology with High-order Fisher Information and Experiments

papers.title: Noise structuring in fixed-depth Trotter simulation: stationary channels and observable-level depolarization
papers.summary: We analyze fixed-depth Trotter simulation as a method for structuring hardware noise in digital many-body dynamics. The number of layers is chosen using the largest endpoint time and is then kept fixed throughout the time scan, making the total noise dose approximately independent of the endpoint time. For local stochastic faults, we show that, once propagated faults lose memory of their insertion layer, the noisy circuit factorizes into ideal evolution followed by a stationary finite-depth binomial channel. In the dilute-layer limit, this channel reduces to a Poissonian exponential. The memory time of a single fault is related to a Loschmidt echo. An important consequence is observable-level depolarization: for selected macroscopic observables at low to moderate noise levels, the stationary channel can act as an almost time-independent affine contrast correction, even though the full channel need not be depolarizing, which is crusial for error mitigation purposes. At short times, the same protocol produces a digital Zeno-like transient, in which a fixed number of noise opportunities competes with a vanishing coherent angle per layer. Our results also reveal limitations of naive zero-noise extrapolatin strategies based on oversimplified functions.

papers.title: Quantum key distribution over a 2 km free-space channel with a high secure key rate
papers.summary: Free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) provides crucial advantages, including mobility and deployment exibility, for securing next-generation communication networks. However, atmospheric turbulence and beam wander severely degrade single-photon coupling effciency and link stability over outdoor channels. In this work, we experimentally demonstrate a free-space decoy-state BB84 QKD system operating at 803 nm with a 100 MHz repetition rate over a 2 km outdoor link. By employing an active beam-wander correction based on fast-steering mirrors (FSMs) and position sensitive detectors (PSDs) with a 500 Hz control loop, we enhance the ?ber coupling effciency and achieve an average ?nite-key secure key rate of 110 kbps with an average quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 3.28 %, representing a 2.5 times secure key rate enhancement under an active beam stabilization. This work demonstrates the indispensability of active beam stabilization and provides an operational reference for robust, long-range free-space quantum communication.

papers.title: Efficient LLM-Generated Shuttling Compilers for Complex Trapped-Ion Architectures
papers.summary: Trapped-ion quantum computers rely on shuttling compilers, which cast an input algorithm into a sequence of ion-qubit movements within a given architecture. We present the first study in which a single frontier large language model (LLM), Claude Opus 4.7, generates and iteratively refines the Python code of shuttling compilers from written specifications. Starting with a compiler for (i) a linear segmented trap, we extend it to (ii) a trap with junctions, and finally achieve efficient compilation for (iii) a broad class of connected trap graphs. The compilers for the more general cases are seeded with code from the previous ones. We benchmark the LLM-generated compilers against state-of-the-art hand-crafted ones using a common suite of quantum circuits. The number of shuttling timesteps is reduced by up to 72% for (i) and up to 43% for (ii). For the broad case (iii) of freely connected architectures, we find large variations in the required number of shuttling timesteps, depending on the connectivity. A densely connected, junction-rich architecture yields up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in shuttling timesteps compared to a corridor-like one. Repeating the complete generation and evaluation with a second frontier LLM, Claude Fable 5, reproduces these findings, with the Fable 5 compilers surpassing the hand-crafted ones more often on the largest circuits. Our results show that an unmodified frontier LLM can produce working, correct, and competitive shuttling compilers without additional manual algorithmic engineering. Generating compilers this way reduces the development time for new architectures from several months to a few days.

papers.title: Exact minimum measurement dependence for faithful local deterministic models of multipartite GHZ-Mermin correlations
papers.summary: A local deterministic model can reproduce Bell-inequality violations only if the hidden state depends on the measurement settings. Hall found the minimum such dependence for the singlet state [Phys. Rev. Lett. 105, 250404 (2010)] and posed the corresponding problem for the Mermin state [Phys. Rev. A 84, 022102 (2011)]. This paper solves it, for the $n$-party GHZ-Mermin scenario at every $n \geq 3$, with the marginals reproduced as well as the correlators. The minimum measurement-dependence fraction is $F_{\min}(n) = R/[2(R+1)]$, with $R = 2^{\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor}$ the Mermin violation ratio: $1/3, 2/5, 4/9, 8/17, \ldots$, always below $1/2$. The lower bound follows from Mermin's inequality by a general overlap bound; the upper bound is an explicit model, uniform on the hidden-variable classes that violate the fewest constraints, with closed-form counts; a reduction theorem shows that for Mermin scenarios the marginals impose no additional dependence. The Mermin values are also certified by integer-arithmetic enumeration through $n = 22$. Every minimal contradiction of size $k$ among stabilizer constraints has correlator-only minimum $1/(k-1)$. With the marginals included the minimum is the same on every core of the $C_5$ ring cluster, on the size-4 and size-5 cores of $C_4$ and on every four-core of $C_6$, but larger on the size-6 and size-7 cores of $C_4$ and on 112 of the 1,920 five-cores of $C_6$, with exact certificates on both sides in every case.

papers.title: Vanilla Exact Synthesis of CNOT Circuits is NP-hard
papers.summary: Exact CNOT synthesis seeks a minimum-size circuit implementing a given invertible binary linear transformation. We study its vanilla formulation: synthesis from the identity on fixed labeled qubits, without ancillas and with all-to-all connectivity. We prove that this problem is NP-hard and that its bounded decision version is NP-complete. Hardness persists even for unitriangular targets that are low-rank perturbations of the identity and under near-linear gate budgets. Our proof gives a polynomial-time reduction from the NP-complete Hamiltonian path problem on grid graphs. A unary hypercube embedding translates graph vertices into circuit parities and edge traversals into CNOT updates. The central challenge is that Hamiltonian paths require intermediate vertex visits, whereas exact synthesis constrains only the final transformation. We bridge this gap with a replicated recorder qubits construction that encodes the required parities in the final outputs, together with a tight gate budget that forces every sufficiently short implementation to trace a Hamiltonian path. Crucially, this path structure is enforced by the construction rather than imposed as a restriction on the circuit. The result directly implies NP-hardness for shortest word problem and Cayley-graph distance computation over $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ with elementary transvections as generators, as well as fixed-width sequential XOR program minimization. For CNOT-minimal exact phase polynomial synthesis, it yields NP-hardness with a zero phase polynomial; extending the reduction to grid-graph Hamiltonian cycle problem establishes hardness even when the final linear transformation is the identity. These complementary results show that the linear and phase components each independently suffice for NP-hardness of exact phase polynomial synthesis.

papers.title: Partial Stabilizer Learning under Fixed Commuting Constraints and the Absence of a Copy-Rate Discount
papers.summary: We consider an unknown pure stabilizer state of \(n\) qudits with a fixed prime local dimension \(p\), together with prescribed commuting Pauli observables. Rather than learning the whole state, the learner must recover only complementary stabilizers that commute with the prescribed observables, together with their eigenvalues. Once the prescribed measurement is performed, this information and the observed outcome determine the corresponding conditional stabilizer state. We compare the number \(k\) of copies available to the learner with the number \(n\) of qudits and refer to their ratio \(k/n\) as the copy rate. Suppose that the dimension \(m\) of the requested complementary stabilizer subspace satisfies \(m=\beta n+o(n)\) for a fixed \(0<\beta\leq1\). If the copy rate converges to a value below one, the optimal exact recovery probabilities and verification scores converge to zero, both in the worst case and under the uniform prior. Conversely, if the number \(k\) of copies minus the number \(n\) of qudits tends to positive infinity, the entire stabilizer state can be identified with probability tending to one, and the requested complementary information can then be extracted. Thus, restricting the learning target to the stabilizer information needed after the prescribed measurement yields no copy-rate discount.

papers.title: Optimal single-copy estimation of quantum state moments: why $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^3)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^4)$ are equally hard
papers.summary: Estimating nonlinear properties of an unknown quantum state with restrictive experimental accessibility is a fundamental problem in quantum learning. We study the sample complexity of estimating the state moments $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^t)$, allowing arbitrary adaptive single-copy measurements. While purity estimation has optimal sample complexity $\Theta(\sqrt d)$ at constant additive error, the optimal dimension dependence for higher moments has remained unclear. We resolve this question for every fixed integer $t\ge 2$: for any sufficiently small constant additive error, the optimal sample complexity is \[ \Theta\!\left(d^{\frac{\lceil\log_2 t\rceil}{1+\lceil\log_2 t\rceil}}\right) \] with constant success probability. The complexity thus follows a dyadic hierarchy: for each integer $h\geq1$, all moment orders $2^{h-1}<t\leq2^h$ share the same exponent. In particular, the third and fourth moments both require $\Theta(d^{2/3})$ copies. Our results also apply to multistate overlaps, weighted and partial-transpose moments, fixed-rank spectrum estimation, and distributed estimation of nonlinear quantities. We also establish an $\Omega(d^{1-1/t})$ lower bound for arbitrary nonadaptive single-copy protocols, matching the known upper bound and demonstrating an advantage from adaptivity for every $t\geq4$. Our upper bound uses adaptive state filtering to reduce higher-order moment estimation to lower-order moment estimation in a smaller state space. For the lower bound, we directly compare moment-matched ensembles through a smooth interpolation, bypassing the maximally mixed state as an intermediate hypothesis and yielding matching bounds beyond $\sqrt d$.

papers.title: Fault tolerance of quantum circuits with tensor networks and symplectic geometry
papers.summary: We develop an operator-algebraic framework for analyzing fault tolerance in quantum circuits and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for exact recovery of the ideal computation under a prescribed noise model. For prescribed circuit families and noise models, we derive a semidefinite program (SDP) based test whose infeasibility certifies that there does not exist any recovery map restoring its intended operation. For non-adaptive stabilizer circuits, analyzing the stabilizer symmetries of its components with symplectic geometry, we obtain closed-form detection and logical-effect matrices that characterize circuit distance algebraically. Applied to a finite Hastings--Haah honeycomb Floquet-code circuit, these matrices certify the dynamical encoding of two logical qubits and distance four under Pauli noise including measurement errors. Using these matrices, we then derive MacWilliams identities for circuit weight enumerators and obtain linear-programming (LP) upper bounds on circuit distance. Output-code constraints give additional Singleton-like bounds. Under independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) depolarizing noise, the weight enumerators determine decoder failure probabilities and yield upper bounds on circuit pseudothresholds. Finally, we derive LP distance bounds for families of flag syndrome-extraction circuits specified by their CNOT orderings, by incorporating the $t$-flag criterion as additional linear constraints to the distance-bounding LP. An analytical CSS Hamming-code benchmark yields a tight distance-three bound attained by the Chao--Reichardt one-flag construction.

papers.title: Geometric heat pumping on a quantum processor
papers.summary: Geometric heat pumping is the transfer of energy between reservoirs at equal temperature where the heat exchanged in an adiabatic cycle depends only on the driving contour in parameter space. We implement this mechanism on a superconducting quantum processor using a collision model, where a driven qubit interacts repeatedly with two ancilla qubits that are prepared in thermal states and emulate the reservoirs. Energy measurements before and after each interaction provide a calorimetric record of the heat exchanged with each reservoir. By reversing the driving contour, we extract a heat contribution associated with pumping. Its dependence on the period and on the contour follows exact simulations of the collision model, without adjustable parameters, and approaches in the slow-driving regime the geometric limit of the corresponding Lindblad dynamics.

papers.title: Sufficient quantum provenance: retained fields and certified recording precision
papers.summary: Quantum executions sharing a provenance record can produce different output distributions. We ask which execution details to retain, and at what precision, to guarantee agreement within a declared Hellinger tolerance. Pairwise separation constraints characterize sufficient field sets on finite context classes, exposing omissions that pass individually but fail jointly. Separately, six-qubit hardware measurements over six tested contexts certify minimum label counts of two for raw outputs and one after a fixed decoder, at tolerance 0.15 with 97\% simultaneous confidence under stationary independent shots. Execution records thereby carry checkable agreement guarantees.

papers.title: Classification of bipartite observables II: NIP observables and the Todorcevic trichotomy
papers.summary: A bipartite observable is stable when its expectation does not depend on which system is idealized first. We show that it is stable exactly when its idealized responses are continuous, and NIP exactly when they are of the first Baire class. For a NIP observable the idealized responses form a Rosenthal compactum, and the dividing lines of Shelah in model theory, together with the classification of Rosenthal compacta of Todor\v{c}evi\'c, acquire a physical meaning. We prove that, for observables, mixtures of states make every hereditarily separable compactum of idealized responses metrizable. The Todor\v{c}evi\'c trichotomy thus becomes a classification into three classes, and we exhibit in each class a physical order: the comparison of photon numbers, the comparison of positions, and the causal order of spacetime, whose idealized responses are not first countable because a light cone can shrink to a point; the comparison of two phases on a circle joins the causal order in the third class. Each of the seven minimal families of the heptachotomy, which Argyros, Dodos and Kanellopoulos extracted from the methods of Todor\v{c}evi\'c, is realized, as we show, by a tree of preparations of photons, of a particle in a box, or of a spin chain read by a probe; the spin chain also reveals that NIP, unlike its uniform version, is not symmetric between the two parties. Finally, for the Ising model in a transverse field we prove that, in the ordered phase, the responses of the two pure phases form split pairs whose midpoints, the responses of the symmetric state, form an uncountable discrete set; the proof rests on a Lee--Yang theorem for this model.

papers.title: An Instability of the Quantum Markov Length
papers.summary: The Markov length, the length scale governing the exponential decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) in a quantum many-body state, has proven useful for characterizing mixed-state phases of matter. Nevertheless, we show that a state's Markov length is not generally stable under weak local channels. The failure of stability occurs already at a pure product state. We demonstrate this explicitly in a one-dimensional fermionic chain, where a fine-tuned depth-two circuit of nearest-neighbor Gaussian channels maps the vacuum to a state whose CMI decays \emph{algebraically} and whose Markov length is therefore infinite, even when the channels are taken arbitrarily close to the identity. The algebraic decay is rooted in the nonanalyticity of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators. We exhibit an analogous instability on an ordinary qubit chain. More generally, we show that the Markov length is unstable in any translation-invariant state with even a single rank-deficient reduced density operator. These results pose a challenge to recent definitions of mixed-state phase equivalence based on the Markov length.

papers.title: Rate and depth of two-axis twisting by pair exchange under the self-Kerr constraint
papers.summary: In this paper, we study two bosonic modes that exchange pairs of quanta, which realize two-axis twisting exactly: within a sector of fixed particle number the exchange operator is proportional to the two-axis twisting generator, with a fixed factor of two. Because any real nonlinear medium supplies a local Kerr nonlinearity alongside this operator, the two merge into one twisting Hamiltonian governed by a single dimensionless ratio $r=\chi_s/\chi_e$ of the Kerr strength to the exchange strength. Two conditions then decide how much of the ideal behavior survives this constraint, and they must be met separately. The first concerns speed: the exponential squeezing rate follows in closed form, vanishes exactly at $r=\pm1$, and recovers as the square root of the distance from that point. The second concerns depth: the smallest attainable squeezing parameter depends only on the anisotropy of the mean-field saddle, attaining the full two-axis-twisting value at $r=0$ and $r=\pm3$ regardless of the rate, so that settings sharing the same anisotropy but differing twofold in rate reach the same depth. The two conditions address different targets, and a system may squeeze quickly yet terminate at a shallow optimum; only $r=0$ is optimal in both respects. The closed-form Gaussian solution reveals a further systematic bias: because the early-time decay rate of the variance exceeds twice the exponential rate, a fit to short-time data overestimates the rate by more than a factor of two. Since an isotropic cubic nonlinearity imposes $r=1$, the value at which the rate vanishes, the two strengths must be mismatched, and a moderate mismatch already restores most of the optimal depth. Finally, the constraint is invisible at low excitation: at two quanta the Kerr term shifts both coupled states equally, so the two Hamiltonians are indistinguishable until four quanta.

papers.title: Photon-stimulated decay of $\chi$-matched ancillas causes unheralded bit flips in bosonic codes
papers.summary: Bosonic codes often read out their syndrome with a transmon ancilla whose computational levels $g$ and $f$ have equal parity and matched dispersive shifts: a decay $f\to e$ is then heralded and leaves the code intact, while the direct $f\to g$ is forbidden by parity. We show that the photons of the code open this decay at first order in the ancilla's decay rate. Dressing by the code mode lets the charge noise that limits the ancilla's $T_1$ drive a photon-stimulated Raman decay $|f,n\rangle\to|g,n+1\rangle$, at $(n+1)(\chi_{ge}/2g_{01})^2$ times the $f\to e$ rate for a smooth noise spectrum. When the matching is set by the detuning, the decay costs $\approx\Gamma_{fe}/\alpha$ per gate and photon, whatever the coupling strength; a deliberate mismatch or matching by a drive lowers this cost, and a qubit ancilla has no such channel. The opened decay is unheralded and flips a cat with probability $\approx 1/2$; being first order, it overtakes the second-order double decay $f\to e\to g$ as the ancilla improves. In a microscopic model of the Ocelot repetition cat code, it makes the bit-flip floor of the gates grow linearly with the cat size, by a factor 1.2-1.7 from four to ten photons, which would limit the noise bias to $\sim 10^3$. The published gate data end at four photons and do not yet test this growth.

papers.title: Scalable Tomography of Coherent Noise via Stabilizer-Code Polarization
papers.summary: Coherent errors accumulate linearly rather than diffusively, making them invisible to Pauli-twirl-based char- acterization. It poses a central challenge for quantum error correction, yet its characterization typically requires multi-qubit process tomography whose cost grows exponentially with system size. We show that measurement- free error correction projects arbitrary few-qubit coherent noise onto a fixed single-logical-qubit effective chan- nel, enabling tomography at constant cost. Exploiting the polarization effects of bit-flip and phase-flip codes, we construct a concatenated effective-channel fingerprint and prove, by a parity-based contradiction argument, that the observation map is globally injective over a prescribed coherent-noise family; hence the underlying noise parameters are uniquely recovered without any sparsity or low-rank assumptions. The recovered coherent noise model can be fed into decoding algorithms; relative to independent noise priors, we expect this to reduce the logical error rate for surface-code decoders. The protocol offers a scalable route to coherent-noise identification whenever the noise admits a moderate-dimensional parameterization.

papers.title: Accurate gap control of 3D-integrated superconducting quantum circuits using asymmetric indium architecture and multi-angle flip-chip bonding
papers.summary: Flip-chip 3D integration is a key enabling technology for overcoming the routing and layout constraints of planar superconducting quantum processors, but it requires accurate and uniform control of the inter-chip spacing while preserving qubit coherence. In conventional processes, thick indium bumps are deposited symmetrically on both chips, while dedicated spacers are introduced to limit the residual tilt. Here, we present a flip-chip bonding process based on an asymmetric indium architecture, combining $20\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ thick indium bumps on the control chip with $200\,\mathrm{nm}$ thin indium pads on the qubit chip. Using electrical and microwave measurements, we demonstrate low resistance and low loss indium interconnects, and show that transmon qubits integrated with this process reach relaxation and coherence times of $T_1=(159\pm14)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $T_{\mathrm{2,echo}}=(294\pm42)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, respectively, comparable to planar devices. Combined with a multi angle compression procedure that suppresses systematic tilt, this approach reduces the average post bonding tilt to $(20\pm12)\,\mu\mathrm{rad}$. These results establish an asymmetric indium architecture combined with multi angle compression as a robust, coherence preserving route toward 3D-integrated superconducting quantum processors.

papers.title: Limits of adaptive two-way linear postprocessing in six-state quantum key distribution
papers.summary: Two-way classical communication improves the noise tolerance of quantum key distribution, but the limits of adaptive parity processing remain unclear. For the six-state protocol with equal three-basis error rate $p\in[p_*,1/2]$, where $p_*=(5-\sqrt5)/10\simeq27.64\%$, we construct a single compatible collective attack that defeats a broad class of linear postprocessing. Each public message may be a linear function of the sender's raw key, chosen adaptively from the public history. For every finite input length and every accepted transcript of positive probability, Eve's optimal probability of recovering any linear function of Alice's raw key is at least Bob's. Consequently, reliable agreement on a linear final key is incompatible with secrecy. The same conclusion holds for arbitrary publicly seeded privacy amplification after reliable recovery of a linear candidate. The proof conditions on the complete transcript, which restricts the two raw keys to affine subspaces. A local degradation of Eve's state, a known R\'enyi-entropy comparison, and a coset-probability inequality then give the recovery comparison. Both inequalities are proved in self-contained appendices. The result allows block splitting, regrouping, nonzero-syndrome selection, and adaptive linear reconciliation.

papers.title: Constrained dissipation and the lifetime of quantum many-body scars
papers.summary: We investigate the fate of quantum many-body scars in the PXP model subject to Markovian dissipation. We show that when local jump operators respect the same symmetries of the Hamiltonian the full Liouvillian spectrum displays a tower of states with properties analogous to standard quantum scars: large overlaps with N\'eel states and equally spaced gaps in the imaginary part of the eigenvalues, set by a single frequency. Whether the long-time dynamics is dominated by scars is determined by the real parts of the eigenvalues, which are set by the ratio between the two relaxation rates $\gamma_{\pm}$ describing spin flips down-to-up or up-to-down respectively. For asymmetric dissipation ($\gamma_+ > \gamma_-$) the scarred eigenvalues have the smallest real parts: the resulting enhanced fidelity oscillations are further stabilized by staggered jump operators. In contrast, replacing the full projection operator in the dissipators with a partial one breaks the symmetries of the problem and is seen to destroy dissipative scars altogether.

papers.title: Tunneling Dynamics and Time Delay in Electron Transport through Time-Dependent Barriers with Finite-Bandwidth Reservoirs
papers.summary: We study a model system consisting of a tunneling barrier driven by an external harmonic field and coupled to two leads with finite bandwidth. It provides a physically consistent definition of the tunneling time inside the barrier by subtracting the time delay associated with the leads from the total time delay. We find that the tunneling time always vanishes for wide/high barriers. Remarkably, the time delay persists even when the barrier becomes static, i.e., in the limit where the modulation frequency vanishes. This indicates that the time delay obtained through the introduction of an external periodic perturbation actually reflects an intrinsic property of the tunneling dynamics, rather than an effect of the external drive or of a particular system. We apply our results to the analysis of tunneling times in optical experiments and find good agreement with the experimental data.

papers.title: Level statistics of the disordered Haldane-Shastry model with $1/r^\alpha$ interaction
papers.summary: Understanding how the interaction range and various types of disorder affect the level statistics of many-body quantum systems, leading to the emergence of many-body localization (MBL), is a challenging open frontier. We find that neither position disorder nor random magnetic fields alone yields pristine Poisson statistics in this system; however, Poisson statistics emerge in their combined presence, suggesting the emergence of MBL when both types of disorder coexist. Interestingly, once random magnetic fields break the $SU(2)$ symmetry, the strength of the position disorder, $\delta$, appears to play an important role, as evidenced by an approximate scaling collapse of the disorder-averaged gap ratios that is parametrized in terms of a single parameter, $\alpha \delta$.

papers.title: Perspective: Quantum Computing on Magnetic Racetrack
papers.summary: Magnetic domain walls have long been pursued as carriers of classical information for storage and processing. With the ability to create, control, and probe domain walls at the nanoscale, they are recently recognized as an ideal platform for studying macroscopic quantum effects and provide a natural blueprint for building scalable quantum computing architectures. In particular, the experimentally demonstrated high mobility of domain walls makes them not only suitable as stationary qubits but also as flying qubits, which may offer advantages over currently explored quantum computing platforms. In this Perspective, we outline our current understanding of the essential ingredients and key requirements for realizing universal quantum computation based on magnetic domain walls. We highlight promising concrete material platforms and identify the experiments that are still needed to advance this concept. We also discuss the potential challenges and point to new opportunities in this emerging research direction at the interface between magnetism and quantum information science.

papers.title: Temporal Interference from Topological Transitions in Monitored Quantum Dynamics
papers.summary: Quantum interference is conventionally associated with the coherent superposition of alternative paths. We uncover a temporal form of interference in repeatedly monitored quantum systems, appearing directly as fringes in the stochastic first-detection-time distribution. This temporal interference becomes remarkably long lived near a class of topological transitions at which a pair of dark states emerges in Hilbert space. Close to such transitions, the corresponding quasi-dark modes dominate the late-time dynamics and interfere coherently, producing pronounced temporal fringes whose decay becomes arbitrarily slow upon approaching the transition. We identify the symmetry conditions underlying this mechanism and relate the fringe frequency to the energy spectrum of the Hamiltonian. Our results reveal how the interplay of quantum superposition, topological transitions, and dark-state formation generates long-lived temporal interference in monitored quantum dynamics.

papers.title: Universal link between structural relaxation and self-diffusion in simple supercooled liquids
papers.summary: Despite a vigorous effort, a comprehensive and satisfactory understanding of the dynamics underlying the glass transition in finite-dimensional systems has not yet emerged. One key hallmark of supercooled liquids approaching the glass transition is the breakdown of the classical Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation, manifested as the decoupling between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time, commonly described by a fractional SE relation. Whether and how the fractional SE exponents vary remains an ongoing debate, even for the simplest supercooled liquids. In this work, we numerically establish a universal relation between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time by introducing characteristic scales that are revealed under the condition of constant dynamical heterogeneity. Moreover, this universal relation could also capture literature data for supercooled water and silica. Remarkably, we find that the fractional SE exponent is invariant across various supercooled liquids studied spanning a wide range of fragility, thereby challenging the prevailing view that the fractional SE exponent is correlated with fragility. Our study demonstrates that investigating dynamical heterogeneity yields more valuable insights into understanding glassy dynamics than expected.

papers.title: Thermodynamics of coupled electromagnetic and mass fields
papers.summary: We formulate a unified thermodynamic framework for chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic transport by extending the Gibbs--Duhem relation to include kinetic free-energy contributions associated with material and field motion. The resulting kinetic Gibbs--Duhem relation establishes a thermodynamic connection between free-energy variations, generalized chemical potentials, pressure, and transport momentum, while preserving the invariance of the system free energy under changes of reference frame. Within a Lagrangian formulation of free-energy evolution, the relation provides a common structure for diffusion, momentum transport, and electromagnetic dynamics. For nonuniform chemical systems, the framework recovers the coupling between Cahn--Hilliard dynamics and the Korteweg stress arising from composition gradients. Its extension to electromagnetic systems incorporates electric, magnetic, charge, and mechanical contributions into the same thermodynamic formulation, yielding a unified description of electromagnetic and momentum evolution. The framework further separates dissipative from nondissipative transport and establishes a common thermodynamic form for mechanical and electromagnetic propagation. In the isentropic limit, the characteristic propagation velocity is determined by the derivative of the thermodynamic pressure with respect to density, yielding the speed of sound for mechanical systems and the speed of light for electromagnetic systems. These results show that kinetic contributions can be incorporated consistently into the Gibbs--Duhem framework, providing a common thermodynamic basis for coupled chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic transport without introducing separate thermodynamic principles for each mechanism.

papers.title: Visualizing surface-reaction-driven chloride migration and cascading failure in sulfide solid electrolytes
papers.summary: Moisture instability of sulfide solid electrolytes limits practical use in all-solid-state batteries. Spatially resolving gas--solid reactions during moisture exposure remains challenging. Here, cryogenic four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (cryo-4D-STEM) maps nanoscale degradation in low- and high-Cl argyrodite electrolytes, Li\(_6\)PS\(_5\)Cl and Li\(_{5.5}\)PS\(_{4.5}\)Cl\(_{1.5}\). Li\(_6\)PS\(_5\)Cl undergoes predominantly surface-localized degradation that progressively extends inward, whereas Li\(_{5.5}\)PS\(_{4.5}\)Cl\(_{1.5}\) exhibits rapid interior amorphization accompanied by outward chloride redistribution. Density functional theory calculations indicate a lower chloride-migration barrier along the modeled pathway in the higher-Cl composition, while chloride removal and vacancy formation distort the PS\(_4^{3-}\) framework and may destabilize the lattice. Surface treatment suppresses detectable large-scale chloride segregation and improves moisture tolerance, retaining 99.9% of the capacity measured at the start of 0.33 C cycling after 150 cycles. These results identify chloride redistribution as a key process in degradation propagation and suggest a route toward moisture-tolerant solid-state batteries.

papers.title: Synergistic Self-Driven Nanoconfinement and Dynamical Heterogeneity in Deeply Supercooled "No Man's Land" Water
papers.summary: The 150--235 K ``no man's land'' (NML) of deeply supercooled water is a highly debated regime where rapid crystallization hinders experimental observation of the hypothesized liquid-liquid phase transition. Using TIP4P/2005 molecular dynamics simulations, we uncover a structurally and dynamically heterogeneous state at ambient pressure that exhibits novel physical features. Our results demonstrate that this low-density state ($\rho \approx 0.925$ g/cm$^3$) is a unique supercooled liquid, distinct from both glassy and spinodal states. Specifically, it emerges as a stable, structurally arrested phase driven by a self-generated ``soft skeleton'' of nanoclusters. This network forms an intrinsic nanoporous structure that imposes nanoconfinement on the remaining fluid, proving that NML confinement can be an entirely self-driven phenomenon. Finally, we resolve the temperature-dependent, nonlinear behavior of density and compressibility, highlighting a structurally driven anomaly that clarifies the thermodynamics of deep supercooling. Collectively, this work provides a transformative structural framework for understanding the anomalous nature of water within the NML.

papers.title: Probing nonequilibrium transport and density profiles in tilted interacting fermion chains with local reservoirs
papers.summary: We investigate how local particle reservoirs can probe transport and density profiles in tilted spinless fermion chains with nearest-neighbor interactions. Using finite-chain Lindblad calculations with particle injection and extraction at opposite ends, we define a threshold-dependent transmission range from the stationary current as the chain length is varied. This range decreases with increasing tilt and follows the trends of the equilibrium density-crossover width in the parameter regimes studied. Interactions can enhance transmission by compensating field-induced energy costs, whereas strongly polarized configurations suppress transport. A third, weakly coupled extraction reservoir provides a complementary spatial probe: its current is exactly proportional to the local occupation in the presence of the probe, and the normalized current approaches the unperturbed nonequilibrium density as the probe coupling vanishes. We illustrate the detection of staggered density modulations and show that bulk densities can continue to relax after boundary currents have nearly stabilized. These protocols connect current measurements to spatial transmission and density structure in driven interacting chains.

papers.title: Anyon bound states in MoTe$_2$ Fractional Chern Insulators
papers.summary: Binding anyons to optically active excitons offers a route to manipulate fractional excitations and reveal the internal spatial structure of anyons. We establish the formation of anyon bound states between a mobile dipolar exciton and an $e/3$ quasihole in a twisted bilayer MoTe$_2$ fractional Chern insulator. Using exact diagonalization of a continuum-based interacting model, we identify a regime of meV-scale binding and strong exciton-quasihole entanglement controlled by exciton mobility and the distance between the exciton and the FCI. Spatial correlations resolve a localized depletion core carrying approximately $e/3$ charge around the exciton, providing a real-space characterization of the bound state. Beyond its fractional charge, the quasihole exhibits a moir\'e-induced octupolar structure. Interlayer tunneling anisotropy strongly deforms this structure while leaving the enclosed charge nearly unchanged, linking the internal profile of the anyon to the underlying electronic quantum geometry. These findings establish conditions for robust exciton-anyon binding in moir\'e heterostructures and show how these composites provide access to properties of fractional excitations beyond their total charge.

papers.title: Fractional Chern insulators and composite Fermi liquids vs. charge order in twisted MoTe$_2$
papers.summary: The bandstructure of twisted MoTe$_2$ around 3.7$^\circ$ consists of spin-valley locked Chern bands with a bandwidth that is smaller than the interaction scale. As such, the strongly correlated phases familiar from Landau levels can be realized: Quantum Hall states, composite Fermi liquids and charge order. These states have in common that they are all favoured by strong interactions, however changing the quantum geometry and topology of the bands as well as their bandwidth via the displacement field and twist angle tilts the balance between them. We provide a comprehensive exact diagonalization analysis of the competition between these states and in particular elucidate the nature of the charge order at fillings $\nu=-\frac14,-\frac13,-\frac12,-\frac23$. Furthermore, we analyze the effect of band mixing by going beyond a single band per valley. This effect of band mixing is crucial for reconciling the numerical phase diagrams with experimental observations.

papers.title: Comment on "Skyrmion Hall Effect in Altermagnets"
papers.summary: In their Letter, Jin et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 196701 (2024)] predict a transverse velocity $v_y$ for skyrmions driven by spin-transfer torque (STT), known as skyrmion Hall effect (SkHE), in d-wave altermagnets. Usually, the SkHE emerges from the skyrmion's topological charge which here cancels between sublattices. Instead, Jin et al. attribute the SkHE to the dimensionless quadrupole tensor $A_{ij}$. The result in their Eq. (12) is fitted to micromagnetic simulations, yielding a finite value for $A_{xy}$. However, via the divergence theorem, $A_{ij}$ simplifies to a boundary integral that vanishes for a sufficiently smooth and localized texture. In this Comment, we substantiate our claim from Ref. [2] that the numerically observed SkHE by Jin et al. for a micromagnetic model with standard Zhang-Li STT in the individual sublattices is merely a discretization artefact.

papers.title: Attraction from repulsion in an interacting Chern band: chiral superconductivity, generalized Hall crystals, and competing fractional Chern insulators
papers.summary: Experiments realizing strong interactions in partially filled Chern bands have observed fractional Chern insulators (FCIs), superconductors, and topological crystals in close proximity. Yet the microscopic relation between them remains poorly understood. Here, we use tensor network simulations to study repulsively interacting spinless fermions in a tunable topological band of the checkerboard lattice. We characterize the competing phases and identify key features of the experimental phenomenology. FCIs from the Jain sequence transition into chiral p-wave superconductivity both below and above half filling as the band dispersion is enhanced. By contrast, at half filling, a generalized Hall crystal with quantized Hall conductance and a doubled unit cell forms for sufficiently strong coupling. Surprisingly, a weak-coupling approach starting from a metallic parent state captures the nature of both ordered phases at intermediate coupling. We find that fluctuations in the metal generate longer-range attraction, which we analyze within the random-phase approximation. This approach captures the pairing symmetry as well as the radial form factors of the Cooper pairs, and incorporating this attraction into Hartree-Fock selects the observed Hall crystal. Together, these results identify fluctuation-induced attraction from repulsion as a common microscopic ingredient of ordering, while our tensor network computations establish the direct competition of both phases with FCIs.

papers.title: Quantum-interference correction to conductivity in disordered electronic bands with non-uniform quantum geometry
papers.summary: Weak localization in two-dimensional disordered electron systems originates from constructive interference between time-reversed scattering paths, giving rise to a logarithmically divergent quantum-interference correction to the dc conductivity. This behavior is generally suppressed when time-reversal symmetry (TRS) is broken. In this study, using a band-projected framework motivated by spin- and valley-polarized rhombohedral $N$-layer graphene (RNG), we show that nonuniform quantum geometry can qualitatively modify quantum-interference corrections to dc transport. In particular, continuously tuning the quantum geometry can change the sign of the conductivity correction, corresponding to a crossover between localization and antilocalization tendencies. Remarkably, at special values of the parameter controlling the quantum geometry, weak-localization (WL) or weak-antilocalization (WAL) can re-emerge despite broken microscopic TRS. At these special points, the orbital structure of the Bloch states gives rise to an emergent antiunitary symmetry that protects a gapless Cooperon mode and restores the logarithmically divergent quantum-interference correction characteristic of WL or WAL. Our results establish nonuniform quantum geometry as a mechanism for controlling quantum interference and electron localization in multiorbital electronic systems.

papers.title: Valley-Selective Transport through Structural Domain Walls in Rhombohedral Graphene Quarter Metals
papers.summary: Domain walls separating quarter metals with opposite valley polarizations have recently been imaged in rhombohedral graphene multilayers. Depending on their formation mechanism, these walls respond in distinct ways to external magnetic probes. Therefore, understanding their behaviors is critical to the interpretation of experimental results. In this work, we examine domain walls formed from strain-induced one-dimensional structural defects that separate domains with complementary rhombohedral stacking orders. We show that while transport across such domain walls is controlled by the valley degree of freedom, the coupling to a magnetic field is dictated by the momentum-space chirality encoded in the Hamiltonian. As a consequence, structural domain walls are rendered electronically opaque by an applied magnetic field, while intrinsic domain walls formed by spontaneous valley symmetry breaking are unstable in the presence of such an ordering field and can be eliminated. This dichotomy allows the two types of domain walls to be distinguished in a magnetotransport experiment.

papers.title: Bulk-Defect Correspondence in Algebraic Classical Spin Liquids
papers.summary: Local constraints in algebraic classical spin liquids give rise to singular momentum-space correlations. This so called pinch-point singularity carries a momentum-space winding number that determines the low-energy structure of the algebraic spin liquid. We show that nonmagnetic vacancies in two dimensions reveal this topological invariant in the real-space winding of the surrounding spin textures. Under explicit conditions, we prove this bulk-defect correspondence for rank-$n$ $\mathrm{U}(1)$ spin liquids and verify it numerically for the Coulomb spin liquids of the kagome and checkerboard lattices and the rank-2 $\mathrm{U}(1)$ spin liquid of the honeycomb-snowflake model. In this way we show that vacancies can be used as general probes for distinguishing the emergent gauge theories of strongly correlated classical disordered magnets.

papers.title: Segregation of cylindrically confined cross-linked polymers
papers.summary: Entropic repulsion between polymer chains under confinement in a narrow channel tends to induce segregation. Recent computer simulation studies have provided indirect evidence that internal cross linking of ring polymers, which creates internal loops, enhances the entropic force. Such topologically enhanced entropic forces are thought to contribute to the segregation of bacterial chromosomes during replication. In this study, we use Monte Carlo computer simulations of a coarse-grained hard-sphere chain model to measure the configurational free energy of two cross-linked ring polymers as a function of the separation distance between the polymer centers of mass. We examine the effects of varying the polymer architecture as well as the confinement dimensions on the free energy functions. In addition, we use the results to make a quantitative assessment of the accuracy of a simple theoretical model built on the de Gennes blob model that has been used in past studies to estimate the overlap free energy of confined polymers. Consistent with indirect evidence from previous simulations studies of segregation dynamics, we find that increasing the number of internal loops and selecting binding sites to enforce a side-loop configuration tends to increase the overlap free energy. Analysis of the whole-polymer and interior-loop extension and overlap lengths reveal a sequence of overlap domains that explain subtle variations in the free energy functions. For all architectures examined, the theoretical model provides a reasonably accurate prediction for how the cross linking and degree of confinement affects the free energy, with quantitative discrepancies comparable to those observed in previous studies using linear polymers and ring polymers without cross links.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Crystal Structural Prototypes: Construction, Classification, and Applications
papers.summary: Crystal structural prototypes describe recurring atomic arrangements across chemically distinct materials. Prototype libraries are built through crystallographic curation, standardization, geometric matching, local-environment clustering, and periodic-graph analysis, and support chemical substitution, derivative enumeration, high-throughput screening, structure solution, crystal structure prediction (CSP), and generative design. This survey compares methods by the structural information they retain and the equivalence rules they impose, distinguishing crystallographic structure types, geometric realizations, chemistry-anonymous topologies, and chemical decorations. We review curated and automatically extracted prototype libraries (AFLOW, CSPD, LAE-ICSPD, EMFDTW, TYPIX, ICSD structure types), their source databases, and algorithms for assigning family membership. A GraphID-based analysis of samples from ICSD, the Materials Project, OQMD, and LeMat shows that the 100 most frequent families in each sample cover 30 to 67 percent of analyzed structures, while 72 to 82 percent of observed families are singletons. The GraphIDs of up to 76 percent of structures change when the neighbor tolerance is varied. In our comparison of 12 generative CSP models, template retrieval achieves the highest top-1 success rate. Removing a reduced-stoichiometry class from training introduces new failures in 50 to 78 percent of the test structures of that class, which measures sensitivity to stoichiometric coverage, not generalization to unseen prototypes. We relate these findings to earlier statistics of structure types, space groups, and periodic nets, and to protein-fold coverage studies. We propose independent-database coverage measurements, discovery-rate analyses, and family-held-out tests to assess how prototype reuse affects prediction accuracy, generalization, and novelty.

papers.title: Zeta potential of magnetic-field-controlled silver nanoparticles
papers.summary: Magnetic-field-dependent nanoparticle size does not by itself determine zeta potential, which also depends on interfacial charge, electrolyte screening, and the location of the slipping plane. We extend the sphere-packing description of silver nanoparticles by distinguishing the structural surface, the effective charge plane, and the hydrodynamic slipping plane. The model uses structural radii of \SI{20}{nm} and \SI{5}{nm} at zero field and \SI{250}{mT}, with reported zeta potentials of \SI{-13.2}{mV} and \SI{-10.0}{mV}. Effective charge is related to the defective-shell atom count. For field-independent interfacial parameters, the linear response without additional charge weighting decreases with decreasing radius. Its normalized form depends on three electrokinetic lengths through only two sums, preventing their independent determination from a field-dependent zeta curve. At \((\kappa^{-1},t_{\mathrm{lig}},\delta_{\mathrm{slip}})=(3,0,1)\,\mathrm{nm}\), nonlinear Poisson--Boltzmann electrostatics changes the fitted shell coefficient from 0.316 to 0.299. Constant total charge still predicts an increase in zeta magnitude, opposite to the observed trend in the evaluated scenarios. Independently calibrated shell and area charge laws differ by less than \SI{0.05}{mV}, so the endpoint agreement does not distinguish these mechanisms. Propagating the initial size frequencies gives a narrower endpoint size distribution than measured. With charge parameters determined from the measured size populations, its predicted mean zeta potential is \SI{-9.131}{mV}, with standard deviation \SI{0.994}{mV}. Imposing the measured mean by charge recalibration does not remove the discrepancy in size width. The combined structural and electrokinetic model thus identifies both the size-dependent contribution to zeta potential and the interfacial information needed to interpret it.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Response Tensors in Crystalline Magnets: Application to Kagome Metals
papers.summary: The prediction of response tensors from magnetic textures is a crucial challenge in the study of noncollinear magnets. Existing methods for constructing descriptors of a given response tensor are limited to first-order multipole expansions or restricted to simple magnetic structures. In this work, we construct a complete symmetry-invariant descriptor basis for arbitrary crystal structures and magnetic textures, providing interpretable features for machine learning modeling of response tensors. We modify the standard principal component analysis framework and derive uncorrelated order parameters that are hierarchically stable: extending the order parameter space to include higher-degree spin order introduces additional order parameters that are uncorrelated to the previous ones. We apply this framework to regression and classification of the anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) in a magnetic kagome lattice. In particular, in the regime where AHC is well modeled by linear regression of the symmetry-invariant order parameters, we find that the squared regression coefficients, ranked by their magnitude, obey a Zipf-like power law: $\beta_{r}^2 \propto r^{-\alpha}$. Our method provides a systematic route to construct interpretable order parameters of all spin orders that connect the symmetry of a magnetic crystal to its response tensors.

papers.title: Generalized length-gauge time-dependent Liouville equation
papers.summary: The length-gauge (LG) time-dependent Liouville equation is a major workhorse to simulate ultrafast dynamics. The equation features the commutator between the density operator $\hat{\rho}$ and the position operator ${\bf r}$, $\langle n{\bf k}|[{\bf r},\hat{\rho}]|m{\bf k}'\rangle$, where $|n{\bf k}\rangle$ and $|m{\bf k}'\rangle$ are Bloch states for bands $n$ and $m$ at crystal momenta ${\bf k}$ and ${\bf k}'$, respectively. This commutator has two irreconcilable versions: Kohn and Luttinger (Phys. Rev. ${\bf 108}$, 590 (1954)) have two partial derivatives with respect to ${\bf k}$ and ${\bf k}'$, but Aversa and Sipe (AS) (Phys. Rev. B ${\bf 52}$, 14636 (1995)) have one partial derivative and one Dirac delta. For several decades, this outstanding discrepancy has received little attention. Here, we show that the generalized LG time-dependent Liouville equation has two partial derivatives, but no Dirac delta. Physically, the ${\bf k}$-off-diagonal matrix elements of the position operator provide a channel by which the electric field generates ${\bf k}$-off-diagonal matrix elements for $\hat{\rho}$ in LG. The discrepancy emerges when the position matrix is assumed to be diagonal in ${\bf k}$. Consequently the AS' equation is a limiting case of our generalized Liouville equation, where the relative momentum ${\bf Q}$ between two states is ignored. Our numerical test reveals that the ${\bf k}$-diagonal formalism yields qualitatively different results and underestimates both energy absorption and polarization by a factor of 7. Our study establishes a general formalism for the length-gauge time-dependent Liouville equation and opens the door for future research on the ultrafast time scale, while prior results based on the ${\bf k}$-diagonal only equation may need to be revisited.

papers.title: Coexistence of Griffiths phase and superparamagnetic-like behavior in La-doped antiferromagnetic CaMnO3
papers.summary: The coexistence of a Griffiths phase and superparamagnetic-like short range interaction in a single-phase homogeneous manganite is of particular interest because it reveals multiple levels of magnetic clustering generated by disorder and competing exchange interactions. In bulk $\mathrm{La}_{0.19}\mathrm{Ca}_{0.81}\mathrm{MnO}_{3}$, this unusual magnetic state develops in the antiferromagnetic regime, where A-site disorder strongly modifies the local magnetic landscape. Rietveld analysis confirms a single-phase orthorhombic structure, while magnetic measurements establish a Griffiths phase below $T_{\mathrm{G}} = 280\text{ K}$ through the deviation from Curie-Weiss behavior. Superparamagnetic-like behavior persisting from 280 to 370 K further indicates that isolated magnetic clusters remain stable well into the nominally paramagnetic region. The presence of both phenomena highlights the crucial role of disorder-induced exchange randomness in stabilizing complex magnetic states in correlated perovskite oxides.

papers.title: Interplay between high-entropy effects and the superionic transition in fluorite oxides: A liquid-like perspective
papers.summary: Minor actinide (MA)-bearing mixed oxide (MOX), a prominent high-entropy ceramic (HEC), is a promising candidate for advanced fast reactor fuels. Using a hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics (MC/MD) approach, we reveal that Np and Am segregation establishes a distinct short-range order (SRO) that induces severe lattice distortion. We uncover a competitive mechanism between localized high-entropy blocking effects and collective superionic dynamics, where the anionic kinetic and structural evolution within the 2000-2800 K range is partitioned and governed by the Tammann crossover temperature and superionic transition temperature. In the low-temperature regime, severe lattice distortions induced by the SRO structures create localized electrostatic and strain-coupled potential wells, which spatially confine the O-ions and lead to their sluggish diffusion. The system exhibits increased dynamical heterogeneity as thermal activation alleviates these structural constraints. Crucially, these localized traps spontaneously transform into a highly interconnected, string-like polyhedral topological network. Driven by the maximization of configurational entropy, this structural change creates low-viscosity transport pathways that trigger confinement-enhanced diffusion. Consequently, a dramatic kinetic inversion occurs, where the O-ion mobility of SRO model surpasses that of random solid solution (RSS) model via an entropy-driven compensation mechanism. Finally, through Gibbs free energy minimization and defect analysis, structural and thermodynamic origins of the superionic transition in HEC are elucidated. This study unveils how local chemical ordering regulates ion transport under extreme conditions, providing theoretical support for the design of high-performance nuclear fuels with both superior radiation tolerance and optimized mass transfer capabilities.

papers.title: Pressure-Dependent hcp-to-fcc Phase Transition Path Derived from Exact Lattice Summations over Inverse Power Law Potentials
papers.summary: We investigate the phase transition between hexagonal close-packed (hcp) and face-centered cubic (fcc) structures along the Burgers-Bain transformation path at pressures up to several hundred gigapascals. We consider a hierarchy of interatomic potentials, from $(n,m)$-Lennard-Jones potentials to extended Lennard-Jones two-body interactions in terms of inverse-power expansions and the Axilrod-Teller-Muto three-body term, alongside density functional theory (DFT) calculations for solid argon. For inverse-power potentials, free energies are evaluated through exact lattice sums and efficient integral representations based on generalizations of the Epstein zeta function to anisotropic interaction kernels, followed by lattice-parameter optimization. This methodology enables an accurate determination of the pressure-dependent Burgers-Bain minimum-energy path and the associated activation barrier for the phase transition. The transformation exhibits pronounced symmetry breaking connecting the Burgers and Bain paths, a feature confirmed by DFT calculations. At high pressure, the hcp-to-fcc activation barrier increases approximately linearly with pressure, owing to the dominant pressure-volume contribution. Including entropy and anharmonic effects yields excellent agreement with experimental temperature-dependent volumes up to the melting point. DFT results also highlight the increasing importance of many-body interactions under compression. Whereas two-body potentials predict that the path passes through the body-centered cubic (bcc) structure only at very high pressures, DFT generally predicts a pathway that bypasses bcc. The Axilrod-Teller-Muto term slightly reduces this discrepancy. Furthermore, DFT performs better at high pressures, where dispersion forces become less important.

papers.title: Adaptive Crack-Tip Localization of Phase-Field Fracture Computations
papers.summary: Phase-field models of fracture provide a unified framework for simulating crack nucleation and propagation, but their computational cost remains high because the governing equilibrium and phase-field equations are typically iteratively solved over the entire domain at every staggered iteration. We present an extension of the recently developed adaptive mesh refinement and coarsening framework that localizes not only spatial resolution but also repeated solution effort to a small active patch around the crack tip for linear elastic brittle materials. The inactive exterior is eliminated through a Schur complement and condensed onto the patch interface, and its factorization is reused as long as the patch remains fixed. The phase field is frozen in the exterior, introducing only a small approximation in the crack wake. The method is implemented in FEniCSx and evaluated for quasi-static crack propagation, dynamic crack branching, three-dimensional mixed-mode crack growth, and coalescence of multiple cracks in a unit cell. Across these problems, the condensed formulation reproduces the reference solutions with differences in global quantities below 0.5%, while substantially reducing the number of active degrees of freedom. In the quasi-static surfing problem, wall time speedups increase from 6.9 to 22.8 as the domain size is doubled, demonstrating increasing computational advantage for large-scale phase-field fracture simulations.

papers.title: Coherent phonons in photoexcited semiconductors from first principles
papers.summary: Coherent phonons are phase-locked lattice vibrations that provide a sensitive probe of nonequilibrium dynamics in materials. Existing first-principles equation-of-motion (EOM) approaches have successfully described coherent phonons in metals and semimetals, but their extension to semiconductors requires treating the long-lived electron--hole plasma created by above-gap excitation. Here we extend the first-principles EOM framework to photoexcited semiconductors by incorporating the residual plasma force that shifts the lattice equilibrium together with the plasma-induced renormalization of the electronic structure. For monolayer MoTe$_2$, the calculated carrier-density-dependent Te displacement agrees with constrained density-functional perturbation theory only when the renormalized band structure is included. We then show that increasing the photoexcited carrier density enhances both the initial total force and the plasma-shifted equilibrium position of the $A_{1g}$ mode, producing larger coherent lattice oscillations. This density-controlled response appears in both the atomic displacement and the coherent-phonon-induced band renormalization, providing complementary signatures for ultrafast reflectivity and time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.

papers.title: From Surface Reactions to Inhibitor Coverage: A Machine-Learning-Assisted Computational Study of Area-Selective Atomic Layer Deposition
papers.summary: Area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) enables selective material growth for the fabrication of nanoscale semiconductor devices. Predicting inhibitor coverage is essential for understanding and optimizing surface blocking in AS-ALD. Here, we present a computational workflow combining a pretrained universal machine-learning interatomic potential with off-lattice grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations and apply it to inhibitor adsorption and precursor blocking on amorphous SiO2. Realistic surface models reveal substantial site-dependent variations in reaction energies and activation barriers, with silanol groups serving as the primary adsorption sites for aminosilane and related inhibitors and metal precursors. Coverage simulations show that inhibitors producing identical adsorbed fragments can yield different coverages because the intact molecules impose distinct steric constraints, leading to different accessible site densities and blocking capabilities. Beyond coverage, we highlight the importance of the reactivity of adsorbed inhibitor fragments toward precursors in determining inhibitor stability and blocking performance. Together, these findings demonstrate the need to consider both steric effects and chemical reactivity on realistic amorphous surfaces. Our calculations connect local reaction chemistry with inhibitor coverage and provide a computational basis for understanding inhibition mechanisms and selecting suitable inhibitor-precursor combinations for AS-ALD.

papers.title: Fully Gapped Superconductivity in the Nonsymmorphic Centrosymmetric Superconductor In2Bi
papers.summary: The nature of superconductivity in nonsymmorphic In2Bi remains an open question, with ongoing debate over whether it exhibits conventional (BCS-like) or unconventional superconductivity. Here we report the physical characteristics and superconducting properties of polycrystalline In2Bi. Measurements of electrical resistivity, magnetization, penetration depth, and specific heat demonstrate the superconducting transition temperature about 6 K, with a sharp transition in resistivity (Delta_Tc = 0.1 K) and RRR = 57.32, reflecting the high quality of the sample. The upper critical field Hc2(0) obtained from resistivity and magnetization measurements are in good agreement with each other and are smaller than the Pauli limit, suggesting orbital limited mechanism. The coherence length = 35.43 nm, penetration depth = 101.9 nm and electron-phonon coupling constant = 1.05 suggest strongly coupled type-II superconductivity. For T<Tc, Delta_lambda(T) is best described by an s-wave BCS model and does not have any power law dependency with T, which is expected for a nodeless superconducting order parameter. The superfluid density reveals a fully gapped superconductivity with a gap of 2Delta_0/kBTc = 4.02. In the superconducting state, the electronic specific heat is best described by an s-wave BCS model with a gap of 2Delta_0/kBTc = 4.05. All these results from the present study indicate that In2Bi is a typical type-II,BCS-like, strongly coupled, and fully gapped superconductor in the dirty limit.

papers.title: Hidden Staggered Superconducting Order in V2Se2O-Family Altermagnets
papers.summary: $\eta$ pairing describes a staggered superconducting condensate whose order parameter changes sign between neighboring unit cells while maintaining a uniform magnitude. Nearly four decades after its theoretical proposal by C. N. Yang, a material platform for stabilizing $\eta$ pairing has remained elusive. Here, we reveal that altermagnetism, despite being pair breaking for conventional BCS pairing, naturally favors $\eta$-like pairing in V$_2$Se$_2$O-family altermagnets. Their valley-contrasting spin structure gives rise to oppositely spin-polarized, symmetry-related valleys centered at $X=(\pi,0)$ and $Y=(0,\pi)$, which form spin-singlet pairing partners separated by the commensurate momentum $\mathbf Q=(\pi,\pi)$, thereby favoring an $\eta$-like condensate. Self-consistent calculations demonstrate that the resulting $\eta$-like state remains robust over broad variations of chemical potential, hopping parameters, and Fermi-surface topology. To detect this hidden staggered order, we propose a phase-sensitive Josephson measurement with a uniform superconductor, where destructive interference suppresses single-Cooper-pair tunneling while preserving two-Cooper-pair processes. This constitutes a charge-$4e$-like Josephson response despite a bulk condensate composed of charge-$2e$ Cooper pairs, providing a direct phase-sensitive signature of the otherwise elusive $\eta$-like condensate in V$_2$Se$_2$O-family altermagnets.

papers.title: Kitaev, semi-Dirac, and spinon quantum spin Hall liquids on the square-hexagon-dodecagon lattice: A parent projective symmetry group classification
papers.summary: The square-hexagon-dodecagon (SHD) lattice hosts an exactly solvable Kitaev spin liquid, while further-neighbor couplings frustrate its Heisenberg magnet into classically degenerate lines where quantum fluctuations can melt the N\'eel order. To place this state among the lattice's spin liquids, we classify fermionic parton mean-field states with singlet and spin-orbit-coupled triplet amplitudes by their projective symmetry groups (PSGs). As SHD sites lack site symmetry, its $Z_2$ PSGs are the projective classes of $p6mm$ with time reversal, from which those of every single-orbit $p6mm$ lattice follow. In the idealized Kitaev model, where lattice operations do not rotate spins, these liquids carry a single $Z_2$ PSG descending from the $SU(2)$ Lieb-flux state, and their projections are exact eigenstates. The PSG's sixfold-rotation sign, fixed by the dodecagon flux, doubles all Majorana bands, and the mirrors exclude a chiral phase in any uniform field, so only a sublattice-staggered three-spin term drives the non-Abelian Ising phase. Beyond the Kitaev state, we find a critical semi-Dirac spin liquid, with mean-field correlations $\propto r^{-3}$ along three directions and $r^{-6}$ otherwise, and extended Dirac phases with up to $48$ fermion flavors, among them an $N_f=12$ state whose PSG forbids every singlet mass. Out-of-plane Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya couplings gap the Dirac states of its $U(1)$ class into a mean-field spinon counterpart of the Kane-Mele quantum spin Hall insulator, with spin Chern number $1$ or $3$ and spin-carrying monopoles. Chiral states imply Kalmeyer-Laughlin, semion$\times$semion, and three-fermion orders, rotation-breaking ones show $q\to -q$ asymmetric neutron spectra, and sign-alternating fluxes break time reversal alone. Masses and monopoles in these many-flavor phases and the energetics of frustrated SHD Heisenberg models are natural next steps.
